exam1.question: In a normal common carotid artery (CCA), the spectral waveform usually shows forward flow throughout diastole. What best explains this?

options.text: The CCA itself has lower peripheral resistance than the internal carotid artery
Most CCA flow continues into the low-resistance internal carotid artery and brain
The external carotid artery supplies a low-resistance bed in the face and scalp
Elastic recoil of the aortic arch reverses flow in early diastole

exam1.explanation: Roughly 70 to 80% of CCA flow normally enters the internal carotid artery, which supplies the low-resistance cerebral circulation, so the CCA waveform shows continuous forward diastolic flow. The external carotid bed is high resistance, so it does not explain the diastolic flow; it actually pulls the CCA waveform toward a slightly more pulsatile shape than the ICA.
exam1.hint: Think about where most of the blood in the CCA ends up and what that vascular bed is like.

exam1.question: In a 30-year-old with no carotid plaque, color Doppler of the carotid bulb shows a brief area of reversed flow along the outer (posterolateral) wall during systole, while flow along the flow divider remains forward. How should this be interpreted?

options.text: Early ulceration of a small plaque in the bulb
Retrograde flow caused by external carotid occlusion
Aliasing caused by a color scale set too low
Normal boundary layer flow separation in the bulb

exam1.explanation: The widened carotid bulb normally produces a zone of flow separation with transient reversal along the outer wall opposite the flow divider. Aliasing would appear as a color wrap in the fastest, central part of the stream rather than a stable reversal zone along the outer wall; loss of this normal separation in older patients can reflect plaque or wall stiffening.
exam1.hint: Consider what happens to flow when a vessel suddenly widens, as the bulb does.

exam1.question: When measuring carotid intima-media thickness (IMT) for cardiovascular risk assessment, which technique is standard?

options.text: Far wall of the distal CCA, from the lumen-intima interface to the media-adventitia interface
Near wall of the proximal ICA, from the outer adventitia to the lumen-intima interface
Far wall of the carotid bulb, including any plaque present at the measurement site
Near wall of the proximal CCA, measured in a transverse view at peak systole

exam1.explanation: IMT is measured on the far wall of the distal CCA, about 1 cm below the bulb, from the leading edge of the lumen-intima interface to the leading edge of the media-adventitia interface, ideally at end diastole. The near wall is less reliable because its interfaces are blurred by gain and reverberation, and plaque is excluded from IMT measurement.
exam1.hint: The wall farther from the transducer gives the clearest double-line pattern.

exam1.question: Which duplex finding best supports ulceration of a carotid plaque?

options.text: A smooth plaque surface with uniform bright echoes and posterior shadowing
A thin, uniform hypoechoic band along the far wall of the CCA
A crater-like excavation in the plaque surface with color flow swirling into it
Spectral broadening in the ICA just beyond the plaque

exam1.explanation: Ulceration is suggested by a well-defined cavity or crater in the plaque surface, ideally confirmed by color flow eddies filling the defect. A smooth, calcified surface argues against ulceration, and spectral broadening beyond a plaque reflects disturbed flow from narrowing rather than a surface defect.
exam1.hint: Look for a break in the plaque surface that blood actually enters.

exam1.question: A symptomatic patient has extensive plaque in the left ICA. Color Doppler shows only a thin thread of flow through a long segment, the peak systolic velocity in the residual channel is 50 cm/s, and the distal left ICA appears much smaller than the right ICA. Which category best fits these findings?

options.text: Near occlusion
Less than 50% stenosis
50% to 69% stenosis
Total occlusion

exam1.explanation: In near occlusion the lumen is so narrow that velocities may be high, low or undetectable, so the diagnosis rests on a markedly narrowed color lumen (a string of flow) and a small distal ICA. The low PSV does not mean a mild stenosis, and the presence of any flow rules out total occlusion.
exam1.hint: Velocity criteria break down when the residual lumen becomes extremely small.

exam1.question: A patient has a confirmed occlusion of the right ICA with a patent external carotid artery. Which right CCA waveform is most expected?

options.text: Low resistance with more diastolic flow than the left CCA
High resistance with less diastolic flow than the left CCA
Tardus-parvus with a delayed systolic upstroke
Continuous, nearly flat flow without a systolic peak

exam1.explanation: With the ICA occluded, the CCA feeds only the high-resistance external carotid bed, so its waveform becomes more pulsatile with reduced diastolic flow compared with the normal side. A tardus-parvus CCA waveform would point to disease proximal to the CCA, not to a distal ICA occlusion.
exam1.hint: Ask which vascular bed the CCA is still supplying after the ICA closes.

exam1.question: In a patient with a chronic ICA occlusion, the ipsilateral external carotid artery shows a low-resistance waveform with prominent diastolic flow. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: A stenosis at the ECA origin producing post-stenotic flow
Reflection of a stenosis in the opposite ICA
Arteriovenous shunting within the scalp
ECA branches are supplying the brain as collaterals via the orbit

exam1.explanation: When the ICA occludes, ECA branches can fill the ophthalmic artery retrogradely and supply the brain, so the ECA takes on a low-resistance, ICA-like waveform (internalization). This makes it easy to mistake the ECA for a patent ICA, so branches and a temporal tap should be used to confirm vessel identity; an ECA origin stenosis would show a focal velocity jump rather than a globally low-resistance signal.
exam1.hint: Consider how the brain recruits a new supply when its usual inflow is blocked.

exam1.question: A patient has a severe ICA stenosis on one side. Velocities in the opposite CCA and ICA are both elevated because of compensatory flow. Which parameter is least affected by this generalized velocity increase and helps avoid overgrading the opposite ICA?

options.text: ICA peak systolic velocity
ICA end-diastolic velocity
ICA/CCA peak systolic velocity ratio
Degree of spectral window filling

exam1.explanation: Compensatory flow raises velocities along the whole carotid system, so absolute ICA PSV and EDV rise even without local narrowing. Because the CCA velocity rises too, the ICA/CCA ratio stays closer to normal, and combining it with gray-scale and color assessment of plaque helps avoid overcalling the stenosis.
exam1.hint: A value that compares two segments cancels out a change that affects both.

exam1.question: A duplex exam 2 days after carotid endarterectomy with patch angioplasty shows a widened bulb and proximal ICA with a large area of swirling, low-velocity flow and reversal along the patched wall. Velocities beyond the patch are normal. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Early recurrent stenosis from myointimal hyperplasia
Expected flow disturbance from the patch-widened lumen
Suture-line pseudoaneurysm requiring urgent repair
Thrombus forming within the endarterectomy site

exam1.explanation: A patch enlarges the bulb and proximal ICA, which exaggerates the normal flow separation and produces swirling, low-velocity flow, while velocities beyond the patch stay normal. A pseudoaneurysm would appear as a sac outside the vessel wall connected by a neck, and myointimal hyperplasia does not develop within 2 days.
exam1.hint: Think about what a wider lumen does to flow patterns, and how soon restenosis can form.

exam1.question: On gray-scale imaging after carotid artery stenting, where is the original atherosclerotic plaque usually seen?

options.text: Compressed against the vessel wall outside the stent struts
Removed completely during stent deployment
Floating freely inside the stent lumen
Dissolved within days by antiplatelet therapy

exam1.explanation: Stenting does not remove plaque; the stent expands and pushes the plaque against the arterial wall, so it remains visible outside the bright, parallel stent struts. Plaque removal happens with endarterectomy, not stenting, and material inside the stent lumen would be abnormal (thrombus or restenosis).
exam1.hint: Compare what a stent does to plaque with what a surgeon does during endarterectomy.

exam1.question: A 45-year-old has a painless, slowly enlarging lateral neck mass. Duplex shows a solid, well-defined mass at the carotid bifurcation that splays the ICA and ECA apart and contains many vessels with low-resistance flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Branchial cleft cyst
Carotid artery aneurysm
Carotid body tumor (paraganglioma)
Reactive cervical lymph node

exam1.explanation: A carotid body tumor is a highly vascular paraganglioma at the bifurcation that characteristically splays the ICA and ECA, with internal low-resistance flow usually fed by ECA branches. A lymph node has hilar vascularity and sits beside the vessels without widening the bifurcation, and an aneurysm is a dilated arterial lumen rather than a solid mass.
exam1.hint: Focus on the location between the two branches and the striking internal vascularity.

exam1.question: The left vertebral artery shows flow reversed throughout the cardiac cycle, directed caudally toward the subclavian artery, and the left brachial pressure is 40 mmHg lower than the right. How is this vertebral flow pattern best classified?

options.text: Normal antegrade vertebral flow with a high-resistance pattern
Partial (transitional) subclavian steal
Vertebral artery origin stenosis
Complete subclavian steal

exam1.explanation: Vertebral flow that is reversed in both systole and diastole is a complete subclavian steal, usually from severe stenosis or occlusion of the proximal subclavian artery. A partial (transitional) steal shows a mid-systolic deceleration or alternating (bidirectional) flow, with antegrade flow persisting for part of the cycle. A vertebral origin stenosis can dampen antegrade flow but does not reverse it.
exam1.hint: Check whether any part of the cardiac cycle still has antegrade vertebral flow.

exam1.question: Which technique is most reliable for locating the extracranial vertebral artery during a carotid duplex exam?

options.text: Angle laterally from a long-axis CCA view to find it between shadowing transverse processes
Follow the most medial branch of the brachiocephalic artery just above the clavicle
Place the transducer over the mastoid process and angle toward the opposite eye
Follow the external carotid artery upward to its largest posterior branch

exam1.explanation: From a longitudinal CCA view, angling slightly laterally and posteriorly shows the vertebral artery and vein running between the transverse processes, whose acoustic shadows interrupt the vessels at regular intervals. The ECA's posterior branches (such as the occipital artery) are not the vertebral artery, and the mastoid approach is not used for the cervical segment.
exam1.hint: Look for a vessel that disappears and reappears at regular bony intervals.

exam1.question: When calculating the ICA/CCA peak systolic velocity ratio, where should the CCA velocity be obtained?

options.text: In the proximal CCA just above the clavicle
Within the carotid bulb at its widest point
In the distal CCA about 2 to 4 cm below the bulb, away from plaque
At the highest velocity found anywhere along the CCA

exam1.explanation: The CCA reference velocity is taken in a straight, disease-free segment of the distal CCA, about 2 to 4 cm below the bulb. Proximal CCA velocities are often higher and disturbed near the origin, which falsely lowers the ratio; the bulb has flow separation and lower velocities, which falsely raise it; and a CCA stenosis jet would not represent normal inflow.
exam1.hint: The reference velocity should reflect undisturbed CCA flow close to the bifurcation being graded.

exam1.question: The right CCA, ICA and ECA all show low-amplitude waveforms with a delayed systolic upstroke, and the right subclavian artery waveform is also dampened. Left-sided waveforms are normal. Where is the most likely lesion?

options.text: Right ICA origin
Brachiocephalic (innominate) artery
Right distal CCA
Right intracranial ICA siphon

exam1.explanation: Tardus-parvus waveforms in both the right carotid and right subclavian systems point to a lesion proximal to where they share a common inflow, which is the brachiocephalic artery. An ICA origin or siphon lesion would not dampen the CCA, ECA and subclavian waveforms.
exam1.hint: Find the one vessel that feeds every dampened artery listed.

exam1.question: A patient with severe heart failure (ejection fraction 15%) has a carotid plaque that narrows the ICA lumen substantially on gray-scale and color imaging, yet the ICA peak systolic velocity is only 105 cm/s and all carotid velocities are low on both sides. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The stenosis must be less than 50% because the PSV is below 125 cm/s
The low velocities indicate bilateral ICA occlusion
The angle correction must have been set below 45 degrees
Low cardiac output can lower velocities and lead to underestimation

exam1.explanation: Velocity criteria assume normal cardiac output; a very low ejection fraction reduces velocities throughout the carotid system, so a significant stenosis may not reach threshold values. Gray-scale and color plaque assessment and the ICA/CCA ratio should be weighed, and the discrepancy noted, rather than relying on PSV alone as option A does.
exam1.hint: Velocity depends on flow, and flow depends on the pump.

exam1.question: Both common carotid arteries show a sharp systolic peak followed by reversed flow throughout diastole. No carotid plaque is seen. Which condition most likely explains this pattern?

options.text: Aortic valve stenosis
Bilateral ICA occlusion
Severe aortic valve regurgitation
Bilateral subclavian steal

exam1.explanation: In severe aortic regurgitation, blood flows back into the left ventricle during diastole, which can produce bilateral holodiastolic flow reversal in the carotid arteries. Aortic stenosis instead produces bilateral delayed, rounded (tardus-parvus) waveforms with forward diastolic flow.
exam1.hint: Think of a central cardiac cause that pulls blood backward during diastole.

exam1.question: A 78-year-old woman has a sharply curved (coiled) mid ICA with no visible plaque. At the curve the peak systolic velocity is 165 cm/s with mild color variation, and velocities return to normal immediately beyond it. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: Velocity elevation from tortuosity and angle, not a stenosis
A 50% to 69% stenosis by SRU velocity criteria
Fibromuscular dysplasia of the mid ICA
Early dissection with an intramural hematoma

exam1.explanation: Curves and coils accelerate flow and make accurate angle correction difficult, so focal velocity increases without plaque or lumen narrowing are usually not stenoses. SRU velocity categories apply to narrowing caused by visible plaque, so grading this as 50% to 69% would overcall the finding.
exam1.hint: Ask whether there is anything actually narrowing the lumen at that spot.

exam1.question: Which change most directly improves axial resolution in a carotid image?

options.text: Increasing the overall receiver gain
Moving the focal zone deeper than the vessel
Decreasing the frame rate
Using a higher-frequency transducer with shorter pulses

exam1.explanation: Axial resolution equals half the spatial pulse length, so higher frequency and fewer cycles per pulse shorten the pulse and improve axial resolution. Focal zone position mainly affects lateral resolution, and gain changes brightness without improving resolution.
exam1.hint: Axial resolution depends on how long the pulse is in space.

exam1.question: A sonographer is imaging a carotid plaque 2.5 cm deep, but the transmit focus is set at 5 cm. What is the main effect on image quality at the plaque?

options.text: Axial resolution is lost because the pulse lengthens
Lateral resolution is degraded because the beam is wider there
Penetration is reduced because the frequency drops
Temporal resolution improves because fewer lines are needed

exam1.explanation: The beam is narrowest at the focus, so lateral resolution is best there; structures well above the focal zone are imaged by a wider beam with poorer lateral resolution. Focus position does not change pulse length, so axial resolution is not the main problem.
exam1.hint: Focusing narrows the beam at one particular depth.

exam1.question: Pulsed-wave Doppler is operating with a pulse repetition frequency (PRF) of 6 kHz. Above what Doppler shift will aliasing occur?

options.text: 3 kHz
6 kHz
12 kHz
1.5 kHz

exam1.explanation: The Nyquist limit is half the PRF, so with a PRF of 6 kHz, Doppler shifts above 3 kHz alias. The PRF itself (6 kHz) is twice the limit, not the limit.
exam1.hint: The Nyquist limit is a simple fraction of the PRF.

exam1.question: Why is aliasing more likely when measuring high velocities in a deep vessel than in a superficial one?

options.text: Attenuation lowers the transmitted frequency at depth
The Doppler angle automatically increases with depth
Longer echo return times limit the maximum PRF and Nyquist limit
The wall filter rises automatically as depth increases

exam1.explanation: Each pulse must return from the sample depth before the next is sent, so deeper gates force a lower maximum PRF and therefore a lower Nyquist limit. Attenuation affects signal strength, not the transmitted frequency setting, and the Doppler angle depends on vessel orientation, not depth.
exam1.hint: Think about how long the system must wait between pulses.

exam1.question: The true Doppler angle to flow is 50 degrees, but the sonographer sets the angle-correction cursor to 60 degrees. How will the displayed velocity compare with the true velocity?

options.text: It will be underestimated by about 30%
It will be overestimated by about 30%
It will be accurate because both angles are 60 degrees or less
It will be overestimated by about 10%

exam1.explanation: The machine divides the measured shift by the cosine of the entered angle; cos 60 is 0.50 while the true cos 50 is about 0.64, so the displayed velocity is about 0.64/0.50, or roughly 1.3 times, the true value. Entering an angle larger than the true angle therefore overestimates velocity, and the error grows quickly at steeper angles.
exam1.hint: Compare the cosines of the two angles.

exam1.question: Compared with color Doppler, which is a main limitation of power (amplitude) Doppler?

options.text: It is less sensitive to slow, low-volume flow
It is more prone to aliasing at high velocities
It is highly dependent on the Doppler angle
It does not display flow direction or velocity

exam1.explanation: Power Doppler encodes the amplitude (strength) of the Doppler signal, so standard power Doppler shows no flow direction or velocity information. In exchange it is more sensitive to slow flow, does not alias and is less angle dependent, so options A to C describe advantages rather than limitations.
exam1.hint: Ask what power Doppler measures instead of frequency shift.

exam1.question: While scanning the right subclavian artery from a supraclavicular approach, a second, identical artery with similar Doppler signals appears deeper, beyond the bright pleural line. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Mirror-image artifact from the strongly reflective pleura and lung
A duplicated subclavian artery variant
Refraction artifact from the clavicle
Side-lobe artifact from the vertebral artery

exam1.explanation: The pleura-lung interface acts as a strong specular reflector, so the system places a copy of the subclavian artery, including its Doppler signal, deeper than the true vessel. A duplicated subclavian artery is not a real variant, and the copy sitting behind a strong reflector at equal distance is the hallmark of mirror artifact.
exam1.hint: Note where the copy lies relative to the bright interface.

exam1.question: During a carotid exam, color fills beyond the vessel walls into surrounding tissue and appears to cover a thin plaque seen on gray scale. Which adjustment is most appropriate?

options.text: Increase the color gain to improve lumen filling
Lower the color velocity scale
Decrease the color gain until color stays within the lumen
Turn the color wall filter off

exam1.explanation: Color bleeding (blooming) beyond the walls is usually caused by excessive color gain and can hide plaque or make a narrowed lumen look normal. Lowering the scale or the wall filter would increase color sensitivity and make the bleeding worse.
exam1.hint: The color is spilling over; reduce whatever is making it too sensitive.

exam1.question: A heavily calcified plaque in the proximal ICA casts a 1-cm acoustic shadow, so no color or Doppler signal can be obtained within it. What is the best next step?

options.text: Report the shadowed segment as occluded
Raise the color gain until color appears in the shadow
Lower the transducer frequency to penetrate the calcium
Try other windows and sample just proximal and distal to the shadow

exam1.explanation: Calcium reflects nearly all of the beam, so the best approach is to image from other angles and assess flow immediately before and after the shadow; a normal, undisturbed distal waveform makes a significant stenosis within a short shadow unlikely. Calling it occluded is wrong when flow is present beyond the shadow, and more gain only adds noise.
exam1.hint: If you cannot see through it, look around it and at what comes out the other side.

exam1.question: Decreasing the dynamic range (compression) on a gray-scale image will have which effect?

options.text: More shades of gray and a softer, lower-contrast image
Fewer shades of gray and a higher-contrast image
Better axial resolution of small structures
Deeper penetration with less attenuation

exam1.explanation: Dynamic range sets how many echo strengths are displayed as distinct gray levels; narrowing it produces a more black-and-white, higher-contrast image. Dynamic range is a processing setting and does not change resolution or penetration.
exam1.hint: A narrower range of displayed echo strengths means fewer gray steps between black and white.

exam1.question: In the most common arrangement, what are the three branches of the aortic arch from proximal to distal?

options.text: Left common carotid, brachiocephalic, left subclavian
Right subclavian, right common carotid, left common carotid
Brachiocephalic, left common carotid, left subclavian
Brachiocephalic, left subclavian, left common carotid

exam1.explanation: The usual arch gives off the brachiocephalic (innominate) artery first, then the left common carotid, then the left subclavian artery. The right subclavian and right common carotid normally arise from the brachiocephalic artery, not directly from the arch.
exam1.hint: Only one side has a shared trunk off the arch.

exam1.question: What is the most common variant of aortic arch branching?

options.text: A shared origin of the brachiocephalic and left common carotid arteries
The left vertebral artery arising directly from the arch
An aberrant right subclavian artery arising as the last arch branch
A right-sided aortic arch with mirror-image branching

exam1.explanation: A common origin of the brachiocephalic and left common carotid arteries (often called a bovine arch) is the most frequent arch variant. A left vertebral artery arising directly from the arch is the next most common, while an aberrant right subclavian artery and a right-sided arch are less frequent.
exam1.hint: The most common variant involves the first two branches sharing a start point.

exam1.question: An aberrant right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria) typically has which origin and course?

options.text: It arises from the right CCA and passes in front of the trachea
It arises as the first arch branch and passes in front of the esophagus
It arises from the brachiocephalic artery and passes behind the clavicle
It arises as the last arch branch and passes behind the esophagus

exam1.explanation: An aberrant right subclavian artery arises from the distal arch beyond the left subclavian artery and crosses to the right, usually behind the esophagus, which occasionally causes dysphagia. Because it does not come off a brachiocephalic trunk, the right CCA then arises separately from the arch.
exam1.hint: It arises in an unusual position and must cross the midline to reach the right arm.

exam1.question: In most people, the vertebral artery first enters the transverse foramina of the cervical spine at which level?

options.text: C3
C6
C7
T1

exam1.explanation: After arising from the subclavian artery, the vertebral artery usually enters the transverse foramen of C6 and ascends through the foramina to C1. It typically passes in front of the C7 transverse process without entering its foramen, although entry at other levels is a recognized variant.
exam1.hint: The lowest cervical transverse foramen is usually traversed only by veins.

exam1.question: The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at which landmark?

options.text: The lower border of the teres major muscle
The lateral border of the first rib
The medial epicondyle of the humerus
The lower border of the clavicle

exam1.explanation: The axillary artery continues as the brachial artery at the inferior border of the teres major muscle. The lateral border of the first rib is where the subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery, which makes it the most tempting distractor.
exam1.hint: The subclavian-to-axillary transition is at the first rib; this next transition lies lower, at the bottom of the axilla.

exam1.question: During pre-operative arterial mapping, two separate arteries of similar size are seen running side by side in the mid upper arm, each with a normal triphasic waveform. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Paired brachial veins mistaken for arteries
A brachial artery pseudoaneurysm
A high bifurcation of the brachial artery (high radial artery origin)
A persistent median artery

exam1.explanation: The brachial artery normally divides just below the antecubital fossa, but a high bifurcation, usually a high origin of the radial artery, is a common variant that produces two parallel arteries in the upper arm. Veins would show venous, not triphasic arterial, signals, and a persistent median artery runs in the forearm.
exam1.hint: The usual division point has simply moved higher up the arm.

exam1.question: In a patient with a long superficial femoral artery occlusion, which artery usually provides the main collateral pathway to the popliteal artery?

options.text: Inferior epigastric artery
Deep femoral (profunda femoris) artery
Superficial circumflex iliac artery
Anterior tibial artery

exam1.explanation: Branches of the deep femoral artery connect with geniculate branches around the knee and are the main collateral route around an SFA occlusion. The anterior tibial artery is a runoff vessel below the popliteal artery, and the inferior epigastric artery supplies the abdominal wall.
exam1.hint: The main collateral source must arise above the occlusion and reach the vessels around the knee.

exam1.question: After arising from the popliteal artery, the anterior tibial artery reaches the anterior compartment of the leg by which route?

options.text: Passing around the lateral malleolus
Running through the adductor hiatus
Coursing medial to the tibia beneath the pes anserinus
Passing through the upper interosseous membrane

exam1.explanation: The anterior tibial artery passes forward through the gap above the interosseous membrane between the tibia and fibula to enter the anterior compartment. The adductor hiatus is where the superficial femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery, higher in the limb.
exam1.hint: Think about the shortest path from the back of the knee into the front of the leg.

exam1.question: Which patient position is generally preferred for an extracranial carotid duplex exam?

options.text: Supine, neck slightly extended, head turned slightly away from the side scanned
Seated upright with the chin flexed down onto the chest
Prone with the head turned toward the side being scanned
Left lateral decubitus with the neck fully rotated upward

exam1.explanation: A supine patient with the neck slightly extended and the head turned a little away from the examined side gives good access to the carotid and vertebral arteries. Excessive rotation or flexion tightens the neck muscles and can compress or distort the vessels and narrow the scanning window.
exam1.hint: The goal is a relaxed, open neck without over-rotation.

exam1.question: Which practice best reduces the risk of shoulder injury for a sonographer performing carotid exams?

options.text: Raising the table so the scanning arm is abducted about 90 degrees
Using a firm pinch grip on the transducer for better control
Keeping the scanning arm close to the body with abduction under about 30 degrees
Reaching across the patient so the monitor stays behind the sonographer

exam1.explanation: Keeping shoulder abduction low (under about 30 degrees) with the arm supported and close to the body reduces strain on the rotator cuff. Sustained 90-degree abduction and reaching are major contributors to shoulder injury, and a pinch grip increases hand and wrist strain.
exam1.hint: The less the elbow lifts away from the body, the less the shoulder works.

exam1.question: During a carotid duplex exam on an outpatient whose neurologic symptoms began this morning, the sonographer finds a mobile, hypoechoic thrombus in the proximal ICA. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Finish the exam and place it in the routine reading queue
Tell the patient to drive to the emergency department
Advise the patient to see the primary physician next week
Notify the physician at once per critical-result policy and document it

exam1.explanation: A mobile carotid thrombus in a patient with acute symptoms is a critical finding that must be reported directly and immediately to the interpreting or referring physician, following lab policy, with the time and person notified documented. Sending the patient off alone or leaving the study in a routine queue delays urgent care.
exam1.hint: Some findings cannot wait for the usual report turnaround.

exam1.question: A patient's neck dressing prevents imaging of the distal left ICA during a carotid duplex exam. How should this be handled?

options.text: Leave the segment out without comment since others were normal
Document that the segment could not be evaluated and the reason
Copy the distal ICA velocity from the patient's prior exam
Estimate the distal ICA velocity from the proximal ICA value

exam1.explanation: Any part of a protocol that could not be completed should be clearly documented, along with the reason, so the interpreting physician and referring clinician understand the exam's limits. Omitting it silently, copying prior data or estimating values would make the record inaccurate.
exam1.hint: The report should tell the reader exactly what was and was not seen.

exam1.question: Under the Spaulding classification, what is the minimum reprocessing needed for a transducer that touched only intact skin during a carotid exam?

options.text: Cleaning followed by low-level disinfection
Cleaning followed by high-level disinfection
Sterilization
Wiping off the gel with a dry towel only

exam1.explanation: A transducer that contacts only intact skin is a noncritical device, which requires cleaning followed by low-level disinfection. High-level disinfection is required for semicritical devices that touch mucous membranes or non-intact skin, such as endocavitary probes.
exam1.hint: Intact skin is an effective barrier, which puts the probe in the lowest risk class.

exam1.question: A duplex exam is requested 1 day after carotid endarterectomy, and the transducer must be placed near the fresh incision. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Use regular multi-use gel directly over the incision
Scan without gel to avoid contaminating the wound
Use a sterile transducer cover and sterile gel
Wipe the incision with alcohol before scanning

exam1.explanation: Scanning near a fresh surgical wound (non-intact skin) calls for a sterile transducer cover and single-use sterile gel to reduce infection risk. Multi-use gel bottles can be contaminated, and scanning without coupling gel produces a nondiagnostic image.
exam1.hint: A fresh incision is not intact skin.

exam1.question: During a standard carotid endarterectomy, what is removed from the artery?

options.text: The whole diseased segment, which is replaced with a vein graft
The plaque with the intima and part of the media, through an arteriotomy
Only the adventitia, to relieve external compression of the lumen
The external carotid artery, to redirect all flow into the ICA

exam1.explanation: In endarterectomy, the artery is opened and the plaque is peeled out along a plane within the media, removing the intima and inner media, and the arteriotomy is closed primarily or with a patch. Replacing the segment with a graft is a different, less common operation used when the artery cannot be endarterectomized.
exam1.hint: The procedure name tells you it works inside the artery wall.

exam1.question: During carotid artery stenting, what is the main purpose of a distal embolic protection device?

options.text: To keep the stent from migrating after deployment
To dilate the stenosis before the stent is placed
To measure the pressure gradient across the stent
To capture plaque debris released during the procedure

exam1.explanation: Crossing, dilating and stenting a carotid plaque can release debris, so a filter or other protection device is placed to trap emboli before they reach the brain. Pre-dilation is done with a balloon, not the protection device.
exam1.hint: The main danger of manipulating carotid plaque is downstream stroke.

exam1.question: A patient has a tender groin mass the day after femoral artery catheterization. Duplex shows a complex, hypoechoic collection beside the common femoral artery with no internal color or spectral Doppler flow, even with a low color scale, and no communication with the artery or vein. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Femoral artery pseudoaneurysm
Iatrogenic arteriovenous fistula
Groin hematoma
Femoral artery dissection

exam1.explanation: A hematoma is an extravascular blood collection with no internal flow and no connection to the vessel, although it can transmit arterial pulsation on palpation. A pseudoaneurysm shows swirling (yin-yang) flow in the sac and a to-and-fro signal in a neck connecting to the artery, and an arteriovenous fistula shows a direct arterial-to-venous jet with arterialized venous flow. Low scale settings help avoid missing slow flow in a pseudoaneurysm.
exam1.hint: Consider what color Doppler would show inside the collection for each option.

exam1.question: Why does an arterial puncture made above the inguinal ligament carry a higher risk of serious bleeding?

options.text: The external iliac artery is hard to compress and bleeding can track into the retroperitoneum
The artery wall above the ligament is thinner than the common femoral segment
The femoral vein lies directly in front of the artery at that level
Blood flow above the ligament is slower, which delays clot formation

exam1.explanation: Above the inguinal ligament the puncture is in the external iliac artery, which lacks the femoral head as a firm backstop for manual compression, so bleeding can spread unseen into the retroperitoneal space. The common femoral artery over the femoral head is the preferred access site for this reason.
exam1.hint: Think about what lies behind the artery that allows effective pressure.

exam1.question: A 70-year-old man describes a 'shade coming down' over his right eye for about 5 minutes, with full recovery. Which artery is the most likely source of the problem?

options.text: Left internal carotid artery
Right vertebral artery
Right external carotid artery
Right internal carotid artery

exam1.explanation: Transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax) is usually caused by emboli to the ophthalmic artery, the first major branch of the ipsilateral ICA, so a right-eye event points to the right ICA. Hemispheric symptoms are contralateral to the diseased carotid, but eye symptoms are on the same side.
exam1.hint: Trace the retina's blood supply back to its parent artery in the neck.

exam1.question: Which group of symptoms most suggests vertebrobasilar (posterior circulation) insufficiency rather than a carotid territory event?

options.text: Transient monocular blindness and opposite-hand weakness
Vertigo with double vision, unsteady gait and slurred speech
Sudden expressive aphasia with right arm weakness
Left face and arm numbness lasting 15 minutes

exam1.explanation: Vertigo, diplopia, ataxia and dysarthria together reflect brainstem and cerebellar ischemia, which is supplied by the vertebrobasilar system. Monocular blindness, aphasia and one-sided face and arm symptoms are classic anterior (carotid) circulation findings.
exam1.hint: Think about the brainstem and cerebellum and what they control.

exam1.question: A 60-year-old reports dizziness and left arm aching when using the left arm overhead. The left brachial pressure is 35 mmHg lower than the right. Which exam is most appropriate?

options.text: Carotid and vertebral duplex with bilateral arm pressures and subclavian assessment
Transcranial Doppler emboli monitoring alone
Upper extremity venous duplex of the left arm
Lower extremity ankle-brachial index testing

exam1.explanation: Arm-exercise dizziness, arm claudication and a large brachial pressure difference suggest subclavian steal, which is evaluated with bilateral arm pressures and duplex of the subclavian, carotid and vertebral arteries to look for vertebral flow reversal. A venous study or ankle testing would not address the suspected arterial steal.
exam1.hint: The symptoms link arm use with posterior circulation symptoms.

exam1.question: A right-handed man has a 15-minute episode of right hand weakness and difficulty finding words that fully resolves. Disease in which artery is most likely responsible?

options.text: Right internal carotid artery
Basilar artery
Left internal carotid artery
Right vertebral artery

exam1.explanation: Right-sided weakness plus aphasia indicates a left (dominant) hemisphere TIA, which is supplied by the left internal carotid artery. Hemispheric carotid symptoms appear on the side opposite the diseased artery, so the right ICA is the most tempting but incorrect choice.
exam1.hint: Decide which hemisphere is affected before choosing the artery.

exam1.question: In most patients, where does the small saphenous vein terminate?

options.text: In the posterior tibial veins at mid-calf
In the popliteal vein within the popliteal fossa
In the common femoral vein at the groin
In the deep femoral vein in the posterior thigh

exam1.explanation: The small saphenous vein ascends the posterior calf and most commonly joins the popliteal vein at the saphenopopliteal junction, a few centimeters above the knee crease. Joining the common femoral vein is the typical termination of the great saphenous vein, not the small saphenous vein.
exam1.hint: Think about which deep vein lies just beneath the posterior knee crease.

exam1.question: Which vein is formed by the union of the femoral vein and the deep femoral (profunda femoris) vein?

options.text: External iliac vein
Great saphenous vein
Popliteal vein
Common femoral vein

exam1.explanation: The femoral vein and the deep femoral vein join in the proximal thigh to form the common femoral vein, which continues as the external iliac vein above the inguinal ligament. The external iliac vein is the continuation of the common femoral vein, not the confluence itself.
exam1.hint: Trace the two thigh veins upward to the first vein they share in the groin.

exam1.question: The soleal sinus veins within the soleus muscle usually drain into which veins?

options.text: Posterior tibial and peroneal veins
Anterior tibial veins
Great saphenous vein
Gastrocnemius veins

exam1.explanation: The soleal sinusoids are large, valveless muscle veins that empty into the posterior tibial and peroneal veins in the deep posterior compartment. The anterior tibial veins lie in the anterior compartment and do not receive soleal drainage.
exam1.hint: The soleus lies in the deep posterior part of the calf, next to which paired deep veins?

exam1.question: During a compression exam of the thigh, at which location is the femoral vein most often difficult to compress, sometimes requiring a hand placed behind the thigh to assist?

options.text: Just below the saphenofemoral junction
At the confluence with the deep femoral vein
Within the adductor (Hunter) canal in the distal thigh
Behind the knee at the popliteal crease

exam1.explanation: In the adductor canal the femoral vein lies deep beneath thick muscle and fascia, so transducer pressure alone may not coapt the walls; counterpressure from behind the thigh often helps. Near the saphenofemoral junction the vein is superficial and usually compresses easily.
exam1.hint: Consider where in the thigh the vein lies deepest beneath the thickest soft tissue.

exam1.question: Which finding is the accepted criterion for normal compressibility of a deep vein on duplex imaging?

options.text: The vein lumen decreases by about half with firm pressure
Color flow fills the lumen completely without compression
The vein diameter increases during a Valsalva maneuver
The vein walls fully coapt in the transverse plane with probe pressure

exam1.explanation: A normal vein collapses completely, with the anterior and posterior walls touching, when gentle transducer pressure is applied in the transverse plane. Partial collapse is abnormal and suggests thrombus, and color filling alone can miss small or nonocclusive thrombus.
exam1.hint: Normal means the lumen disappears entirely, not just shrinks.

exam1.question: How many veins normally accompany each of the posterior tibial, anterior tibial and peroneal arteries in the calf?

options.text: One single vein
Two paired veins
Three veins
A variable plexus without named veins

exam1.explanation: The deep calf veins are paired venae comitantes, with two veins running on either side of each tibial and peroneal artery. A single accompanying vein is typical of the popliteal and femoral segments, not the calf.
exam1.hint: Calf deep veins are described as venae comitantes; think about how many usually travel with each artery.

exam1.question: At the ankle, where is the great saphenous vein normally located?

options.text: Anterior to the medial malleolus
Posterior to the lateral malleolus
Deep to the Achilles tendon
Between the tibia and fibula

exam1.explanation: The great saphenous vein begins from the medial end of the dorsal venous arch and passes anterior to the medial malleolus before ascending the medial leg. The small saphenous vein, by contrast, starts behind the lateral malleolus.
exam1.hint: Recall the classic ankle site used for a saphenous vein cutdown.

exam1.question: With the patient prone and the transducer in the popliteal fossa, how is the popliteal vein normally positioned relative to the popliteal artery?

options.text: Deep to the artery, closer to the femur
Medial to the artery at the same depth
Superficial to the artery, closer to the transducer
Lateral to the artery, separated by the tibial nerve

exam1.explanation: From a posterior approach the popliteal vein lies superficial to the popliteal artery, so it appears nearer the transducer on the image. The artery lies deeper, against the posterior femur and knee joint capsule.
exam1.hint: Consider the order of structures from the skin of the back of the knee toward the bone.

exam1.question: Which set of Doppler features describes a normal common femoral vein signal in a supine patient breathing quietly?

options.text: Spontaneous flow that varies with respiration
Continuous flow with no respiratory variation
Pulsatile flow that reverses with each heartbeat
No flow until the calf is compressed

exam1.explanation: Normal proximal leg veins show spontaneous flow that is phasic, slowing with inspiration and increasing with expiration as abdominal pressure changes. Continuous, nonphasic flow suggests obstruction between the probe and the heart.
exam1.hint: Normal proximal venous flow responds to the breathing cycle.

exam1.question: What happens to venous outflow from the legs during deep inspiration in a supine patient, and why?

options.text: It increases because intrathoracic pressure falls
It increases because the diaphragm lowers abdominal pressure
It does not change because leg veins have valves
It decreases because the descending diaphragm raises abdominal pressure

exam1.explanation: As the diaphragm descends on inspiration, intra-abdominal pressure rises and compresses the IVC, so flow from the legs slows or stops and then increases on expiration. The fall in intrathoracic pressure on inspiration increases flow in the upper extremity veins, not the leg veins.
exam1.hint: Leg veins must pass through the abdomen before reaching the chest.

exam1.question: What is the normal Doppler response at the common femoral vein when a patient performs a Valsalva maneuver and then releases it?

options.text: Flow becomes pulsatile during the strain phase
Flow stops during the strain and then surges on release
Flow increases during the strain and stops on release
Flow reverses for several seconds during the strain

exam1.explanation: Valsalva raises intra-abdominal pressure, so antegrade flow ceases (with competent valves allowing at most a very brief reversal) and then increases sharply when the breath is released. Prolonged reversal during the strain indicates valvular incompetence, not a normal response.
exam1.hint: Bearing down acts like a temporary dam above the groin.

exam1.question: Both common femoral veins are compressible but show continuous, nonphasic flow that does not change even with deep breathing. Where is the obstruction most likely located?

options.text: Right heart, from severe tricuspid regurgitation
Neither; this is normal in a shallow breather
Inferior vena cava
Both popliteal veins

exam1.explanation: Bilateral loss of respiratory phasicity points to an obstruction central to both groins, most often the IVC (thrombus or extrinsic compression) or bilateral iliac disease. Tricuspid regurgitation makes femoral signals pulsatile rather than continuous, and popliteal obstruction lies distal to the probe, blunting augmentation rather than phasicity. Persistence of continuous flow during deep breathing argues against shallow respiration as the cause.
exam1.hint: Find the one vessel that both legs drain through.

exam1.question: How does respiration normally affect flow in the subclavian and other upper extremity veins?

options.text: Flow decreases on inspiration as abdominal pressure rises
Flow is constant and unaffected by breathing
Flow increases on inspiration as intrathoracic pressure falls
Flow reverses on inspiration because of valve closure

exam1.explanation: In the arms, inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure and draws blood toward the heart, so flow increases; this is the opposite of the leg veins. Upper extremity veins near the chest also show cardiac pulsatility from their proximity to the right atrium.
exam1.hint: Arm veins drain directly into the chest rather than through the abdomen.

exam1.question: During a venous duplex exam, squeezing the calf produces no increase in flow at the femoral vein, although the femoral vein itself compresses normally. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: Obstruction between the calf and the femoral vein
Normal finding in a well-hydrated patient
Incompetent valves in the femoral vein
Obstruction of the iliac vein above the probe

exam1.explanation: Distal augmentation pushes blood toward the probe, and a blunted or absent response suggests an obstruction between the compression site and the sampling site, such as popliteal or calf vein thrombosis. Iliac obstruction lies above the probe and affects phasicity rather than distal augmentation.
exam1.hint: Augmentation tests the pathway between the squeeze and the transducer.

exam1.question: A patient had a right femoral artery catheterization 2 days ago. The right common femoral vein signal is strongly pulsatile, while the left common femoral vein is normally phasic. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Tricuspid regurgitation
Congestive heart failure
Iliac vein compression
Arteriovenous fistula at the puncture site

exam1.explanation: An iatrogenic arteriovenous fistula sends arterial pressure into the adjacent vein, producing local pulsatile, often high-velocity venous flow on the affected side only. Tricuspid regurgitation and heart failure cause pulsatility in both legs, not just one.
exam1.hint: A one-sided change right after an arterial puncture points to a local cause.

exam1.question: Which statement about venous valves in the lower extremity is correct?

options.text: They are most numerous in the common iliac veins
They are more numerous in distal veins than proximal veins
They normally have three cusps like the aortic valve
They open during calf muscle relaxation to allow reflux

exam1.explanation: Venous valves are bicuspid and become more numerous toward the foot, where hydrostatic pressure is greatest; the IVC and common iliac veins usually have none. Valves close, not open, to prevent retrograde flow when the calf muscle relaxes.
exam1.hint: Valves are concentrated where gravity places the greatest load on the column of blood.

exam1.question: A postpartum woman has a painful, markedly swollen left leg that appears pale and white. Pedal pulses are present. Duplex shows occlusive thrombus in the left iliac and femoral veins. Which term best describes this presentation?

options.text: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens
Phlegmasia alba dolens
Venous gangrene
Superficial thrombophlebitis

exam1.explanation: Phlegmasia alba dolens ('painful white inflammation') is extensive iliofemoral DVT with a pale, swollen leg while arterial inflow is preserved. Phlegmasia cerulea dolens is the more severe form with a cyanotic, blue limb and threatened perfusion.
exam1.hint: The color of the limb is the key to the name.

exam1.question: An outpatient with mild calf pain has isolated thrombus in one peroneal vein, with no proximal extension and no strong risk factors. The clinician chooses not to anticoagulate. Which follow-up is commonly recommended?

options.text: No further imaging is needed
Venography within 24 hours
Serial duplex imaging over about 2 weeks to detect extension
Repeat duplex in 6 months

exam1.explanation: For selected low-risk patients with isolated distal DVT who are not anticoagulated, guidelines suggest serial duplex imaging over the next 2 weeks, because propagation into the popliteal vein usually occurs early. A scan at 6 months would miss early extension, the main risk.
exam1.hint: The danger with calf thrombus is early propagation toward the knee.

exam1.question: A patient has a tender, red cord in the posterior calf, and duplex shows noncompressible thrombus in the small saphenous vein extending upward. Which area is most important to examine carefully for possible deep extension?

options.text: The saphenopopliteal junction and popliteal vein
The saphenofemoral junction and common femoral vein
The anterior tibial veins
The posterior arch vein at the ankle

exam1.explanation: Thrombus in the small saphenous vein can extend through the saphenopopliteal junction into the popliteal vein, so the junction and popliteal vein must be imaged closely and the distance of the thrombus tip documented. The saphenofemoral junction is the route of extension for great saphenous vein thrombus.
exam1.hint: Follow the involved superficial vein to the deep vein it empties into.

exam1.question: Which combination of mechanisms is mainly responsible for post-thrombotic syndrome?

options.text: Arterial insufficiency and lymphatic obstruction
Arteriovenous shunting through dilated perforators
Increased capillary permeability from heart failure
Valve damage causing reflux plus residual venous obstruction

exam1.explanation: After DVT, recanalization often destroys valves, causing reflux, and residual scarring can leave outflow obstruction; together they create ambulatory venous hypertension, leading to edema, skin changes and ulceration. Arterial insufficiency is not part of the post-thrombotic mechanism.
exam1.hint: Think about what thrombus and its healing do to the vein lumen and its valves.

exam1.question: A 66-year-old woman has a shallow, irregular ulcer above the medial malleolus with surrounding hyperpigmentation, and her clinician plans multilayer compression bandaging. Which test should be performed before compression is applied?

options.text: Venography of the iliac veins
Serum D-dimer level
Ankle-brachial index to check for arterial insufficiency
Lymphoscintigraphy

exam1.explanation: Strong compression can worsen ischemia in a limb with peripheral artery disease, and mixed arterial-venous ulcers are common in older patients, so an ABI is obtained first. Full compression is generally avoided when the ABI is below about 0.8 and is contraindicated with severe disease (below about 0.5). Venography, D-dimer and lymphoscintigraphy do not address the safety of compression.
exam1.hint: Compression squeezes every vessel in the leg, not just the veins.

exam1.question: When performing a lower extremity venous duplex exam for DVT, how should compression maneuvers be performed along the deep veins?

options.text: In the transverse plane at intervals of no more than about 2 cm
In the longitudinal plane at the groin and knee only
In the transverse plane every 10 cm
Only where color flow appears abnormal

exam1.explanation: Compressions are done in the transverse view at short intervals, generally every 1 to 2 cm, so that short segments of thrombus are not skipped. Compressing in the longitudinal plane risks the vein sliding out of view and appearing falsely compressed.
exam1.hint: Short thrombus segments can hide between widely spaced compressions.

exam1.question: A patient with long-standing venous insufficiency has firm, indurated, brownish skin of the lower medial leg with narrowing just above the ankle, giving the leg an inverted champagne-bottle shape. What is this condition called?

options.text: Lymphedema
Corona phlebectatica
Cellulitis
Lipodermatosclerosis

exam1.explanation: Lipodermatosclerosis is chronic fibrosis of the skin and subcutaneous fat from sustained venous hypertension, producing a hard, pigmented, constricted lower leg. Corona phlebectatica is a fan of small dilated intradermal veins around the ankle, not induration.
exam1.hint: The champagne-bottle shape results from scarring and contraction of the tissue beneath the skin.

exam1.question: An emergency department performs a limited two-region compression exam at the common femoral and popliteal veins, which is negative. Symptoms persist. Which follow-up is generally recommended when the calf veins were not evaluated?

options.text: No further testing, because calf DVT never matters
Repeat the limited exam in about 1 week, or perform a full-leg exam
Start anticoagulation for 3 months without further imaging
Order an arterial ankle-brachial index

exam1.explanation: A limited two-region exam can miss calf DVT that later propagates, so a negative study is usually followed by a repeat exam in about 5 to 7 days (or a D-dimer-guided strategy), or a complete exam including the calf is performed. Treating without a diagnosis exposes the patient to unnecessary bleeding risk.
exam1.hint: The limited exam's blind spot is a thrombus that has not yet reached the knee.

exam1.question: Why is lack of compressibility, rather than visualization of echoes within the vein, the primary criterion for acute DVT?

options.text: Acute thrombus can be nearly anechoic and look like flowing blood
Acute thrombus is always highly echogenic and easy to see
Compression dislodges thrombus and confirms it is acute
Gray-scale imaging cannot show the vein walls

exam1.explanation: Fresh thrombus is often hypoechoic or anechoic and can be invisible on gray scale, so the inability to coapt the walls is the most reliable sign. Highly echogenic material is more typical of older, organized thrombus.
exam1.hint: Ask whether a fresh clot is always visible on the image.

exam1.question: A patient has a tender, red, palpable cord along the medial thigh, and duplex confirms thrombus in the great saphenous vein well away from the saphenofemoral junction. What else should the exam include?

options.text: Nothing further, since superficial clots do not involve deep veins
An ankle-brachial index of both legs
Evaluation of the deep veins, since concurrent DVT is common
Imaging of the contralateral great saphenous vein only

exam1.explanation: Superficial vein thrombosis is associated with coexisting DVT in a substantial minority of patients, often in a noncontiguous segment, so the deep system should be evaluated. Assuming the deep veins are spared risks missing a clot that needs anticoagulation.
exam1.hint: Superficial and deep thrombosis share the same risk factors.

exam1.question: Why is phlegmasia cerulea dolens considered a limb-threatening emergency?

options.text: The thrombus is confined to the calf veins and embolizes easily
Massive venous outflow obstruction raises tissue pressure enough to impair arterial inflow
It causes acute arterial embolism from the heart
It always produces a large pulmonary embolism

exam1.explanation: In phlegmasia cerulea dolens, near-total venous outflow obstruction causes severe edema and high compartment pressures that compromise capillary and arterial perfusion, leading to venous gangrene. It is not caused by an arterial embolus, even though the limb becomes ischemic.
exam1.hint: Consider what happens to inflow when blood cannot leave the limb.

exam1.question: A patient with a prior left femoral DVT has new leg pain. The baseline duplex 6 months ago showed residual wall thickening in the femoral vein but a fully compressible popliteal vein. Which finding today best supports new acute thrombosis?

options.text: Echogenic wall thickening in the femoral vein
Small collateral veins near the femoral vein
A thin echogenic web in the femoral vein lumen
A noncompressible popliteal vein segment

exam1.explanation: New noncompressibility in a segment that was normal on the baseline study is the clearest evidence of recurrent acute DVT. Wall thickening, webs and collaterals are expected residual post-thrombotic findings and do not indicate new clot.
exam1.hint: Compare today's scan with the baseline: what has changed?

exam1.question: During a standing reflux exam, release of calf compression produces 0.7 seconds of retrograde flow in the great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction. How should this be interpreted?

options.text: Normal, because reflux is defined as more than 1 second in all veins
Normal, because any reflux in a superficial vein is expected
Indeterminate, because reflux cannot be judged at a junction
Abnormal, because it exceeds 0.5 seconds for a superficial vein

exam1.explanation: For superficial veins, retrograde flow lasting more than 0.5 seconds is considered pathologic reflux. The longer 1 second threshold applies to the femoral and popliteal veins, not to the great saphenous vein.
exam1.hint: Reflux cut-offs differ between superficial veins and the femoropopliteal deep veins.

exam1.question: An outpatient has mild leg swelling, a low clinical pretest probability of DVT, and a negative high-sensitivity D-dimer test. What is the usual implication?

options.text: DVT is effectively excluded and duplex is usually not needed
Bilateral full-leg duplex is required urgently
The patient should start anticoagulation
Contrast venography is indicated

exam1.explanation: A negative high-sensitivity D-dimer has a high negative predictive value, so in a low-probability patient it essentially rules out DVT without imaging. D-dimer is not useful to rule in DVT, so a positive result, not a negative one, would prompt duplex.
exam1.hint: D-dimer is a sensitive but nonspecific test.

exam1.question: When measuring segmental limb pressures, what is the effect of using a blood pressure cuff that is too narrow for the limb?

options.text: Falsely low pressure
No effect if the Doppler signal is strong
Falsely high pressure
Loss of the Doppler signal

exam1.explanation: A narrow cuff cannot transmit its pressure fully to the artery, so more pressure is needed to occlude flow and the reading is falsely elevated. The cuff bladder should be about 20% wider than the limb diameter; an overly wide cuff tends to read falsely low.
exam1.hint: Think about how much cuff pressure reaches the artery when the cuff is too small.

exam1.question: Right leg segmental pressures are: high thigh 165 mmHg, above-knee 158 mmHg, below-knee 112 mmHg, ankle 104 mmHg. Brachial pressure is 140 mmHg. Where is the most significant disease located?

options.text: Aortoiliac segment
Distal superficial femoral or popliteal artery
Tibial arteries below the calf cuff
Common femoral artery

exam1.explanation: The 46 mmHg drop between the above-knee and below-knee cuffs exceeds the usual 20 to 30 mmHg threshold and localizes disease to the distal superficial femoral or popliteal artery. The normal high-thigh pressure, above brachial, argues against aortoiliac or common femoral disease.
exam1.hint: Find the pair of adjacent cuffs with the largest pressure drop.

exam1.question: Using a four-cuff technique, a patient's high-thigh pressure is 115 mmHg with a brachial pressure of 150 mmHg. Which statement best interprets this finding?

options.text: Normal, since thigh pressure is usually lower than arm pressure
Suggests inflow (aortoiliac) disease, though combined proximal SFA and profunda disease can look the same
Isolates disease to the popliteal artery
Indicates tibial artery occlusion

exam1.explanation: With a narrow four-cuff technique, normal high-thigh pressure is typically 20 to 30 mmHg higher than brachial, so a low value suggests aortoiliac inflow disease. Because the cuff sits over the proximal thigh, disease of both the proximal superficial femoral and deep femoral arteries can produce the same result.
exam1.hint: Normal high-thigh pressure, measured with a narrow cuff, exceeds arm pressure.

exam1.question: Which toe-brachial index (TBI) is generally considered normal?

options.text: 1.3 or greater
Between 0.2 and 0.3
About 0.4
0.7 or greater

exam1.explanation: Toe pressures are normally somewhat lower than arm pressures, and a TBI of about 0.7 or greater is generally accepted as normal. Values around 0.2 to 0.3 indicate severe disease, and toe arteries rarely calcify enough to produce falsely high indices like 1.3.
exam1.hint: Normal digital arteries add some resistance, so toe pressure is not expected to equal arm pressure.

exam1.question: The common femoral artery Doppler waveform is monophasic with a delayed systolic upstroke and rounded peak on both sides. What is the most likely location of disease?

options.text: Aortoiliac segment, proximal to the probe
Popliteal artery, distal to the probe
Tibial arteries
Deep femoral artery only

exam1.explanation: A dampened (tardus-parvus type) monophasic waveform with a slow upstroke indicates significant obstruction proximal to the sampling site, so bilateral changes at the groin suggest aortoiliac disease. Distal disease raises resistance and tends to keep a sharp upstroke rather than delay it.
exam1.hint: A delayed upstroke reflects a problem upstream of the probe.

exam1.question: Reactive hyperemia testing is used as an alternative to treadmill exercise. How does it stress the circulation?

options.text: It raises systemic blood pressure through isometric exercise
It cools the limb to cause vasoconstriction
A thigh cuff occludes flow for several minutes, and the resulting ischemia dilates the distal vascular bed
It uses a vasoconstricting drug to increase peripheral resistance

exam1.explanation: Inflating a thigh cuff above systolic pressure for about 3 to 5 minutes causes ischemic vasodilation, so on release distal resistance falls as it would with exercise, revealing pressure drops across significant lesions. Cold exposure is used for vasospastic testing, not to unmask occlusive disease.
exam1.hint: The test mimics the drop in resistance that occurs in exercising muscle.

exam1.question: Which is a commonly used standard constant-load treadmill protocol for lower extremity arterial exercise testing?

options.text: 6 mph at 0% grade for 1 minute
1 mph at 20% grade for 20 minutes
4 mph at 5% grade for 10 minutes
2 mph at 12% grade for up to 5 minutes

exam1.explanation: A common constant-load protocol walks the patient at 2 mph on a 12% grade for up to 5 minutes or until symptoms force a stop, then measures ankle pressures. The other settings are not standard and are either too strenuous or too prolonged for patients with claudication.
exam1.hint: The protocol is a slow walk up a moderate incline for a few minutes.

exam1.question: When recording pulse volume recordings (PVR) with an air plethysmograph, to approximately what pressure is the cuff usually inflated?

options.text: About 65 mmHg, enough to contact the limb without occluding flow
About 20 mmHg above systolic pressure
Exactly the brachial systolic pressure
About 200 mmHg in all patients

exam1.explanation: PVR uses a low, standardized cuff pressure, commonly about 60 to 65 mmHg, so the cuff senses volume changes with each pulse without stopping arterial flow. Inflating above systolic pressure would occlude the artery and abolish the waveform being recorded.
exam1.hint: The cuff must sense pulsations, not stop them.

exam1.question: What causes the brief reversed-flow component seen in a normal triphasic femoral artery waveform at rest?

options.text: An arteriovenous connection near the knee
Low resistance in the resting muscle bed
High peripheral resistance in the resting muscle bed
A proximal stenosis that creates turbulence

exam1.explanation: At rest, the arterioles of the leg muscles are constricted, creating high peripheral resistance that causes reflected waves and brief flow reversal in early diastole. Low-resistance beds, such as exercising muscle, produce continuous forward diastolic flow instead.
exam1.hint: Compare this waveform with what happens after exercise, when the reversal disappears.

exam1.question: Before measuring a resting ankle-brachial index, how long should the patient rest supine?

options.text: No rest is needed if the patient walked slowly to the room
About 5 to 10 minutes
About 30 seconds, just long enough to place the cuffs
No rest is needed if the patient is seated rather than supine

exam1.explanation: Standard ABI technique calls for about 5 to 10 minutes of supine rest. Even a short walk can lower ankle pressures in patients with PAD, producing a falsely low ABI, and a seated position adds hydrostatic pressure at the ankle, producing a falsely high ABI.
exam1.hint: Even a short walk can temporarily lower ankle pressures in a patient with PAD.

exam1.question: A 74-year-old diabetic smoker reports burning pain in his forefoot that wakes him at night and is relieved when he hangs his foot over the side of the bed. What does this symptom represent?

options.text: Ischemic rest pain from severe arterial insufficiency
Intermittent claudication
Venous insufficiency
Restless leg syndrome

exam1.explanation: Ischemic rest pain occurs when perfusion is inadequate even at rest; it worsens when supine and improves with dependency because gravity increases perfusion pressure. It indicates chronic limb-threatening ischemia, which is more advanced than claudication, which occurs only with exercise.
exam1.hint: Gravity helps arterial flow when the foot hangs down.

exam1.question: In a patient with acute limb ischemia, which finding indicates an immediately threatened limb that needs urgent revascularization?

options.text: Audible pedal arterial Doppler signals
Mild coolness of the foot with normal sensation
Pain with walking only
Loss of sensation beyond the toes and muscle weakness

exam1.explanation: Sensory loss extending beyond the toes and motor weakness indicate an immediately threatened limb (Rutherford class IIb), requiring urgent revascularization. Audible pedal arterial signals with intact sensation and strength indicate a viable limb.
exam1.hint: Nerve and muscle function are the most sensitive markers of severe ischemia.

exam1.question: A 70-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation develops sudden, severe pain and pallor of the right leg. She had no prior claudication, and the left leg pulses are normal. Which cause is most likely?

options.text: Thrombosis of a preexisting atherosclerotic stenosis
Popliteal artery entrapment
Arterial embolism
Deep vein thrombosis

exam1.explanation: Abrupt onset in a patient with atrial fibrillation, no history of claudication and normal pulses in the opposite leg is classic for embolism. In situ thrombosis usually occurs in a patient with prior claudication and bilateral disease, with collaterals that make onset less abrupt.
exam1.hint: Consider the cardiac rhythm and the absence of prior arterial symptoms.

exam1.question: In the lower extremity, where does an arterial embolus most commonly lodge?

options.text: Mid superficial femoral artery
Common femoral artery bifurcation
Dorsalis pedis artery
Proximal external iliac artery

exam1.explanation: Emboli tend to lodge where arteries branch and the lumen narrows abruptly, and the common femoral bifurcation is the most frequent site in the leg. A mid-SFA location is more typical of atherosclerotic disease, especially at the adductor canal.
exam1.hint: Consider where the lumen size changes abruptly in the proximal leg.

exam1.question: A 32-year-old man who smokes heavily has painful ulcers on several toes and a history of migratory superficial thrombophlebitis. Duplex shows normal proximal arteries with segmental tibial artery occlusions, and angiography shows corkscrew-shaped collaterals. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Atheroembolism
Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease)
Popliteal artery entrapment
Raynaud phenomenon

exam1.explanation: Buerger disease affects young smokers, involves small and medium distal arteries and veins, and features migratory thrombophlebitis and corkscrew collaterals. Atheroembolism also causes painful toes but typically occurs in older patients with a proximal atherosclerotic source and palpable pulses.
exam1.hint: Young age, heavy tobacco use and involvement of both arteries and veins are key.

exam1.question: A 68-year-old man has sudden painful blue discoloration of several toes on one foot, with palpable pedal pulses and a normal ABI. Which additional duplex evaluation is most useful?

options.text: Aorta, iliac and femoral arteries to look for an embolic source
Deep veins of the calf for thrombosis
Digital arteries after cold immersion
Great saphenous vein for reflux

exam1.explanation: Blue toe syndrome with palpable pulses suggests atheroembolism (microemboli of cholesterol or plaque debris), so the proximal arteries should be examined for ulcerated plaque or aneurysm as the source. Cold immersion testing evaluates vasospasm, which would not explain sudden unilateral painful cyanosis.
exam1.hint: Small emboli usually come from somewhere upstream.

exam1.question: In the most common form of popliteal artery entrapment syndrome, what is the abnormal anatomic relationship?

options.text: The popliteal artery passes lateral to the lateral head of the gastrocnemius
The popliteal artery is compressed by a Baker cyst
The popliteal vein crosses anterior to the artery
The popliteal artery passes medial to the medial head of the gastrocnemius

exam1.explanation: In the classic forms of popliteal entrapment, the artery takes an abnormal course medial to, and is compressed by, the medial head of the gastrocnemius or an abnormal muscle slip. A Baker cyst can compress vessels but is an acquired mass, not entrapment syndrome.
exam1.hint: The culprit is a calf muscle head on the inner side of the knee.

exam1.question: A 58-year-old man reports buttock and thigh claudication and erectile dysfunction, and both femoral pulses are absent. Which condition is most likely?

options.text: Bilateral popliteal artery aneurysms
Tibial artery disease
Aortoiliac occlusive disease (Leriche syndrome)
Bilateral superficial femoral artery occlusion

exam1.explanation: The triad of buttock and thigh claudication, impotence and absent or diminished femoral pulses describes Leriche syndrome from distal aortic or bilateral iliac occlusion. Superficial femoral artery occlusion typically causes calf claudication with normal femoral pulses.
exam1.hint: Symptom level points to the level of disease; buttock pain means very proximal disease.

exam1.question: In patients with atherosclerotic peripheral artery disease, which is the most common site of occlusive disease in the lower extremity?

options.text: Distal superficial femoral artery at the adductor canal
Deep femoral artery
Dorsalis pedis artery
Proximal common iliac artery

exam1.explanation: The distal superficial femoral artery at the adductor canal is the most frequent site of lower extremity atherosclerotic occlusion, which is why calf claudication is the most common presentation. The deep femoral artery is relatively spared and often serves as an important collateral pathway.
exam1.hint: Calf claudication is the most common symptom; think about the segment above it.

exam1.question: Which pattern of lower extremity arterial disease is most typical in patients with diabetes?

options.text: Isolated aortoiliac disease with normal tibial arteries
Predominantly infrapopliteal (tibial) disease with medial calcification
Aneurysmal dilation of the femoral arteries
Disease limited to the common femoral artery

exam1.explanation: Diabetic PAD typically involves the tibial and peroneal arteries, often with medial (Monckeberg) calcification that can make ankle pressures falsely high. Isolated aortoiliac disease is more typical of younger smokers without diabetes.
exam1.hint: Consider why ankle pressures can be unreliable in diabetic patients.

exam1.question: In an adult, an abdominal aortic aneurysm is most commonly defined as an infrarenal aortic diameter of at least which size?

options.text: 2.0 cm
3.0 cm
4.0 cm
5.5 cm

exam1.explanation: An infrarenal aortic diameter of 3.0 cm or more is the widely used definition of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. A 5.5 cm diameter is the usual threshold for elective repair in men, not the definition of an aneurysm.
exam1.hint: Think of the size used to label a screening scan positive, not the size that triggers surgery.

exam1.question: Segmental pressures show below-knee pressures of 150 mmHg on the right and 120 mmHg on the left. The above-knee and high-thigh pressures are similar on both sides, and the brachial pressure is 135 mmHg. How is the side-to-side difference best interpreted?

options.text: A normal finding, because side-to-side differences are not meaningful
Significant disease on the left between the above-knee and below-knee cuffs
Significant disease on the right, because its pressure is higher than brachial
Aortoiliac disease affecting both legs equally

exam1.explanation: A horizontal (side-to-side) difference of more than about 20 mmHg at the same level points to obstruction on the lower-pressure side, and because the left thigh pressures match the right, the lesion lies between the left above-knee and below-knee cuffs. A below-knee pressure higher than brachial on the right is normal, not a sign of disease.
exam1.hint: Compare the two legs at the same level, then look at which segment the lower side first diverges in.

exam1.question: Under current US Preventive Services Task Force recommendations, which patient should be offered one-time ultrasound screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm?

options.text: A 58-year-old man who currently smokes
A 70-year-old woman who has never smoked
An 80-year-old man who has never smoked
A 68-year-old man who smoked for 20 years and quit 10 years ago

exam1.explanation: The USPSTF recommends one-time AAA screening for men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked, which includes former smokers. A 58-year-old smoker is below the screening age range, and screening is not recommended for women who have never smoked.
exam1.hint: Check both the age window and the smoking history, including past smoking.

exam1.question: A 45-year-old mechanic who often strikes tools with the heel of his right hand has cold, painful ring and little fingers with small fingertip ulcers. Duplex shows a focal aneurysm with mural thrombus in the distal ulnar artery over the hook of the hamate, and the superficial palmar arch is poorly perfused. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Primary Raynaud phenomenon
Thromboangiitis obliterans
Hypothenar hammer syndrome
Arterial thoracic outlet syndrome

exam1.explanation: Repeated blunt trauma to the hypothenar eminence injures the superficial ulnar artery where it crosses the hook of the hamate, causing aneurysm or thrombosis with emboli to the ulnar-side fingers. Primary Raynaud phenomenon does not cause a focal aneurysm or ulcers, thoracic outlet compression involves the subclavian artery, and thromboangiitis obliterans causes segmental occlusions in smokers rather than a focal ulnar aneurysm.
exam1.hint: Link the patient's work habit to the artery lying just under the heel of the hand.

exam1.question: The day after a transradial cardiac catheterization, the radial pulse cannot be felt at the wrist, but the hand is warm and pink. Duplex shows echogenic material filling the radial artery at the puncture site with no flow, and the radial artery just distal to it at the wrist has reversed flow. What do these findings indicate?

options.text: A normal radial artery with an incorrectly set color scale
Radial artery occlusion, with the distal radial artery filled backward through the palmar arch
A radial artery pseudoaneurysm
An arteriovenous fistula between the radial artery and its veins

exam1.explanation: Thrombosis at the access site is the most common complication of transradial access, and an intact palmar arch fills the radial artery beyond the occlusion with reversed flow from the ulnar side. A pseudoaneurysm would show a sac with swirling flow, and a fistula would show high-velocity flow into a vein.
exam1.hint: Ask how flow could reach the wrist from the other direction.

exam1.question: An asymptomatic 71-year-old man has an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 4.3 cm. Under Society for Vascular Surgery guidelines, what is the recommended ultrasound surveillance interval?

options.text: Every 12 months
Every 3 years
