exam2.explanation: The small saphenous vein arises from the lateral side of the dorsal venous arch (lateral marginal vein), passes behind the lateral malleolus and ascends the posterior calf toward the popliteal fossa. The great saphenous vein passes in front of the medial malleolus, and the posterior tibial veins run behind the medial malleolus.
exam2.hint: The two saphenous veins start on opposite sides of the foot and pass opposite surfaces of the ankle bones.

exam2.question: A patient has a painful, red cord in the forearm at the site of a recent peripheral IV. Duplex shows noncompressible thrombus in the forearm cephalic vein, with no extension toward the axillary vein. How is this classified?

options.text: Superficial vein thrombosis (superficial thrombophlebitis)
Upper extremity deep vein thrombosis
Catheter-related central vein thrombosis
Thrombosis of the radial artery

exam2.explanation: The cephalic and basilic veins are superficial veins, so thrombus confined to them is superficial vein thrombosis, commonly caused by infusion. It becomes a concern for deep extension only if it approaches the junction with the axillary or brachial veins.
exam2.hint: Decide whether the cephalic vein belongs to the superficial or the deep system.

exam2.question: A 38-year-old woman has a stroke with no clear cause. Carotid duplex shows no atherosclerotic plaque, but a thin, shelf-like linear projection arises from the posterior wall of the proximal ICA bulb, with a small area of slow, swirling flow just above it. There is no double lumen. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Reverberation artifact
Ulcerated plaque
Spontaneous ICA dissection
Carotid web

exam2.explanation: A carotid web is a thin, fixed, shelf-like intimal projection from the posterior bulb, considered a variant of fibromuscular dysplasia, and the stagnant flow above it can form thrombus that embolizes in young patients. A dissection usually shows a longer flap, a false lumen or a tapering lumen rather than a short fixed shelf.
exam2.hint: A short, fixed membrane at the back of the bulb in a young stroke patient without plaque.

exam2.question: When measuring a great toe pressure with a small digital cuff and a PPG sensor, at what point is the systolic toe pressure recorded?

options.text: When the PPG waveform first disappears as the cuff is inflated
When the PPG waveform reaches its largest amplitude during deflation
When the cuff pressure equals the brachial diastolic pressure
When the PPG waveform first reappears as the cuff is slowly deflated

exam2.explanation: The digital cuff on the proximal phalanx is inflated until the PPG tracing becomes flat, then slowly deflated, and the pressure at which pulsatile flow returns is the systolic toe pressure. Reading at the point of disappearance during inflation is less reliable because inflation is rapid and overshoot is common.
exam2.hint: Systolic pressure is read the same way as with a Doppler probe at the ankle.

exam2.question: Which definition is most widely used for an arterial aneurysm?

options.text: A permanent focal dilation at least 50% larger than the expected normal diameter of that artery
Any artery measuring more than 1 cm in diameter
A dilation at least 10% larger than the adjacent normal segment
Any artery whose wall contains calcified plaque

exam2.explanation: An aneurysm is generally defined as a focal dilation 1.5 times or more the normal diameter of the vessel, so the threshold depends on which artery is involved. A smaller increase is called ectasia, and a fixed size such as 1 cm would be meaningless across arteries of different sizes.
exam2.hint: The definition is relative to the normal size of that artery.

exam2.question: A woman at 34 weeks of pregnancy lies supine. Her left common femoral vein is compressible but shows continuous flow with little phasicity. When she turns onto her left side, the flow becomes normally phasic. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Occlusive thrombus is present in the left iliac vein
Tricuspid regurgitation develops late in pregnancy
An arteriovenous fistula has formed in the groin
The gravid uterus compresses the pelvic veins or IVC when she lies supine

exam2.explanation: In late pregnancy the uterus can compress the IVC and iliac veins in the supine position, damping phasicity; turning to the left side relieves the compression and restores normal flow. A thrombus would not resolve with a position change, so the iliac veins should be examined if the pattern persists.
exam2.hint: Note what changed when only her position changed.

exam2.question: At a severe ICA stenosis, a mosaic of random color pixels appears in the soft tissue around the artery during systole, while the gray-scale tissue looks normal. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Excessive gray-scale gain
Tissue vibration from turbulent flow through the stenosis
A pseudoaneurysm next to the stenosis
Mirror-image artifact from the jugular vein

exam2.explanation: High-velocity turbulent flow makes the surrounding tissue vibrate, and the Doppler system shows this as color speckle outside the vessel, a sign that often accompanies severe stenosis or a fistula. A pseudoaneurysm would show a defined sac with organized swirling flow.
exam2.hint: The color appears outside the vessel only when a jet is strongest.

exam2.question: Which statement about ultrasound contrast agents (gas-filled microbubbles) is correct?

options.text: They stay in the vascular space, are not nephrotoxic, and the gas is exhaled through the lungs
They diffuse into the interstitial space, like iodinated CT contrast
They require kidney function testing before every injection
They are best imaged with a high mechanical index to preserve the bubbles

exam2.explanation: Microbubble agents are pure blood-pool agents that remain intravascular; their gas is exhaled through the lungs and the shell is metabolized, so they are not nephrotoxic. A high mechanical index destroys microbubbles rather than preserving them.
exam2.hint: Think about the size of the bubbles and how the gas leaves the body.

exam2.question: Eight months after carotid endarterectomy with a prosthetic patch, a patient has a pulsatile mass in the neck. Duplex shows a perivascular sac with swirling red-blue flow connected to the patch site by a narrow neck that has to-and-fro flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Pseudoaneurysm at the patch suture line
Carotid body tumor
Recurrent stenosis from intimal hyperplasia
Thrombosis of the internal jugular vein

exam2.explanation: A sac with swirling flow linked to the artery by a neck with to-and-fro flow is the classic pseudoaneurysm pattern; after patch angioplasty it may follow suture failure or infection. A carotid body tumor is a solid vascular mass splaying the bifurcation rather than a sac with to-and-fro neck flow.
exam2.hint: Look at the flow pattern in the channel connecting the sac to the artery.

exam2.question: A 62-year-old smoker has classic calf claudication after walking one block, but his resting ankle-brachial index is 0.98 on both sides. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Report the study as normal and stop testing
Measure ankle pressures and the ABI after treadmill exercise
Repeat the resting ABI with the patient seated
Perform a venous duplex exam for deep vein thrombosis

exam2.explanation: A moderate stenosis with good collaterals can produce a normal resting ABI, and exercise lowers peripheral resistance to reveal a pressure drop across the lesion. Seated pressures are invalid because hydrostatic pressure raises the ankle reading.
exam2.hint: Some lesions only become significant when flow increases.

exam2.question: Eight years after an aortobifemoral bypass, a patient has a painless, pulsatile left groin mass. Duplex at the femoral anastomosis shows a sac outside the graft with swirling color flow that communicates with the anastomosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Graft limb occlusion
Normal postoperative perigraft seroma
Anastomotic pseudoaneurysm
Arteriovenous fistula at the anastomosis

exam2.explanation: Late separation of the suture line or degeneration of the host artery at a prosthetic anastomosis, most often at the femoral level, produces a pseudoaneurysm with a swirling yin-yang sac. A seroma has no internal flow, and an arteriovenous fistula would show high-velocity flow into an adjacent vein rather than a sac.
exam2.hint: Focus on flow outside the graft that connects to the suture line.

exam2.question: A young weightlifter has episodes of arm swelling and distended veins when he lifts overhead. With the arm at his side, subclavian vein flow is normal and phasic. With the arm abducted above 90 degrees, flow becomes continuous and then stops, returning when the arm is lowered. The vein contains no thrombus. What do these findings most suggest?

options.text: Acute subclavian vein thrombosis
A fixed central venous stenosis
Positional venous thoracic outlet compression
Arterial thoracic outlet syndrome

exam2.explanation: Flow that is normal at rest but obstructed only in abduction points to dynamic compression of the subclavian vein at the costoclavicular space; some compression can occur in healthy people, so findings are matched to symptoms. A fixed stenosis or thrombus would alter flow even with the arm at the side.
exam2.hint: Note that the abnormal flow appears only with one arm position.

exam2.question: In a tortuous ICA, color changes from red to blue with a thin black band between the two colors where the vessel curves. How should this be interpreted?

options.text: A change in flow direction relative to the beam, not aliasing
A flow void caused by plaque
Aliasing caused by a color scale set too low
A short occlusion at the curve

exam2.explanation: When the flow direction passes 90 degrees to the beam, the Doppler shift falls to zero, leaving a black band, and the color changes because the direction relative to the transducer has reversed. Aliasing changes color through the brightest hues at the scale limit without a black band.
exam2.hint: Look at what lies between the two colors.

exam2.question: Immediately before an ultrasound-guided thrombin injection begins, which Universal Protocol step should the team perform?

options.text: Schedule the follow-up duplex exam for 24 hours later
Have the sonographer review prior reports alone
Mark the opposite limb to show it is not the target
Pause for a time-out to confirm the correct patient, procedure and site

exam2.explanation: The Universal Protocol requires a time-out just before the procedure in which the team confirms the correct patient, procedure and site. Marking the opposite limb is incorrect; the procedure site itself is marked.
exam2.hint: This step is a final team check right before the procedure starts.

exam2.question: A patient had coronary bypass with the left internal mammary artery grafted to the LAD. He now has chest pain when he works with his left arm. The left vertebral artery flow is reversed, and the left brachial pressure is 45 mmHg lower than the right. Which phenomenon best explains his chest pain?

options.text: Coronary-subclavian steal through the mammary artery graft
Carotid steal through the circle of Willis
Arterial thoracic outlet compression
Isolated vertebrobasilar steal

exam2.explanation: The left internal mammary artery arises from the subclavian distal to the stenosis, so arm exercise can reverse flow in the graft and divert blood away from the heart, causing angina. Vertebrobasilar steal causes neurologic, not cardiac, symptoms.
exam2.hint: Trace where the bypass graft takes its origin.

exam2.question: In a healthy supine adult, the ankle systolic pressure is normally slightly higher than the brachial systolic pressure. What is the main reason?

options.text: Amplification of the pressure pulse as it travels into smaller, stiffer distal arteries, with reflected waves adding to systolic pressure
Gravity increases arterial pressure at the ankle when supine
The ankle arteries have lower resistance than the brachial artery
Blood viscosity is higher in the lower extremities

exam2.explanation: As the pulse travels distally, wave reflection and narrower, less compliant arteries amplify the systolic peak, so a normal ABI is about 1.0 to 1.4. Gravity does not explain it in the supine position, because the ankle and heart are at the same level.
exam2.hint: The shape of the pulse wave changes as it moves away from the heart.

exam2.question: A patient reports cramping pain in the arch of the foot when walking that goes away with rest. Disease at which level most likely explains this symptom?

options.text: The aortoiliac segment
The tibial and pedal arteries
The common femoral artery
The proximal superficial femoral artery

exam2.explanation: Claudication usually appears in the muscle group one level below the obstruction, so foot claudication suggests infrapopliteal (tibial and pedal) disease, as seen in thromboangiitis obliterans and diabetes. Aortoiliac disease causes buttock, hip or thigh pain, and femoral disease mainly causes calf pain.
exam2.hint: Symptoms appear in the muscles just downstream from the blockage.

exam2.question: A woman at 30 weeks of pregnancy has left leg swelling. The femoral and popliteal veins compress normally, but left common femoral vein flow is continuous and stays that way when she lies on her left side. The right side is phasic. What is the best next step?

options.text: Examine the left iliac veins directly and advise further imaging if they cannot be seen well
Report a negative exam because the deep veins compress normally
Repeat the duplex exam 3 months after delivery
Examine only the calf veins for isolated thrombus

exam2.explanation: DVT in pregnancy favors the left leg and the iliac veins, which may be missed by compression of the groin and below. Persistent continuous flow after relief of uterine compression suggests a proximal obstruction, so the iliac veins should be imaged and MR venography considered if they are not seen.
exam2.hint: The position change has already ruled out the simple explanation for the abnormal signal.

exam2.question: Before a vascular exam, a patient says she has a severe latex allergy. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Use latex-free gloves, transducer covers and supplies, and document the allergy
Proceed with latex gloves if the sonographer washes hands first
Cancel the exam, because ultrasound cannot be done safely
Give an antihistamine and proceed with the usual supplies

exam2.explanation: Patients with latex allergy should be examined with latex-free gloves, covers and other supplies, and the allergy should be clearly documented. Ultrasound can be performed safely once latex exposure is avoided, so canceling is unnecessary.
exam2.hint: Remove the source of exposure rather than treating the reaction.

exam2.question: A 75-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation has sudden, severe abdominal pain that is out of proportion to her physical exam. If an embolus has entered the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), where does it most often lodge?

options.text: Right at the SMA origin, flush with the aorta
In the celiac trunk before the SMA
Only within the small distal jejunal branches
A few centimeters beyond the SMA origin, near the middle colic artery

exam2.explanation: SMA emboli typically lodge a few centimeters past the origin, near the middle colic branch where the artery narrows, often sparing the proximal jejunum. Thrombosis of a preexisting atherosclerotic plaque, by contrast, usually occurs at the SMA origin.
exam2.hint: An embolus travels downstream until the artery tapers at a major branch point.

exam2.question: Which practice is standard for screening transcranial Doppler in children with sickle cell anemia (HbSS)?

options.text: Begin screening only after a first clinical stroke
Measure peak systolic velocity under sedation every 5 years
Measure TAMMV in an awake child, screening yearly from about age 2 to 16
Begin screening at age 18 when windows are better

exam2.explanation: STOP-based screening uses the time-averaged mean of the maximum velocity, obtained in an awake, nonsedated child, because sedation and sleep alter cerebral blood flow and velocities. Annual screening from age 2 to 16 is the goal so that high-risk children are found before a first stroke.
exam2.hint: The point of screening is primary prevention, and sedation changes the velocities being measured.

exam2.question: When measuring ankle systolic pressure with a continuous-wave Doppler, what is the effect of deflating the cuff too quickly?

options.text: The systolic pressure is overestimated because the cuff stays inflated too long
The diastolic pressure is recorded instead of the systolic pressure
There is no effect, as long as the probe angle is correct
The systolic pressure is underestimated because the cuff falls below the true pressure before the first signal is heard

exam2.explanation: Deflation at about 2 to 3 mmHg per second lets the first returning Doppler signal be matched to the cuff pressure; with fast deflation the reading lags and is lower than the true systolic pressure. A too-narrow cuff, not deflation rate, causes falsely high readings.
exam2.hint: Think about where the cuff pressure is by the time the first signal is recognized.

exam2.question: In an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm, which finding best distinguishes a dissection flap from laminated mural thrombus?

options.text: It is thick and crescent-shaped and lines the aneurysm wall
It is thin and mobile, with flow on both sides of it
It has flow only on the side facing the center of the lumen
It stays fixed to the wall throughout the cardiac cycle

exam2.explanation: A dissection flap is a thin intimal membrane that moves with each heartbeat and separates two flow channels. Laminated mural thrombus is thick, crescentic and fixed to the wall, with flow only on its luminal side, and echogenic layers within thrombus are a common mimic of a flap.
exam2.hint: Check what lies on each side of the structure and how it behaves with each beat.

exam2.question: A patient has varicose veins and a fan-shaped pattern of many small intradermal veins over the medial ankle and foot (corona phlebectatica), without pigmentation, eczema or ulcer. Under the 2020 CEAP update, what is the clinical class?

options.text: C4c
C1
C3
C4a

exam2.explanation: The 2020 CEAP revision added corona phlebectatica as subclass C4c because it signals more advanced disease. C1 includes only telangiectasias and reticular veins, and C4a refers to pigmentation or eczema, which this patient does not have.
exam2.hint: The 2020 revision gave this ankle sign its own subclass within the skin-change category.

exam2.question: Which hepatic venous finding most strongly supports Budd-Chiari syndrome?

options.text: Absent or reversed hepatic vein flow with comma-shaped intrahepatic venous collaterals
A triphasic hepatic vein waveform with a small reversed a wave
Mildly dilated hepatic veins with normal phasic flow toward the heart
Hepatopetal main portal vein flow with normal respiratory variation

exam2.explanation: Budd-Chiari syndrome is hepatic venous outflow obstruction, shown by absent, flat, or reversed hepatic vein flow and intrahepatic collaterals that bypass the blocked veins. A triphasic waveform with a small a wave is normal hepatic vein flow.
exam2.hint: Look for the option showing blocked venous outflow and a way around it.

exam2.question: A 42-year-old with a stroke has transcranial Doppler monitoring of the MCA while agitated saline is injected into an arm vein. Several microembolic signals appear within seconds after the patient releases a Valsalva maneuver. What does this indicate?

options.text: A right-to-left shunt, such as a patent foramen ovale
Thrombus in the left atrial appendage
Embolism from an ulcerated carotid plaque
Air trapped under the transducer

exam2.explanation: Agitated saline bubbles are filtered by the lungs, so bubbles reaching the MCA must bypass the pulmonary circulation through a right-to-left shunt, most often a PFO. Releasing Valsalva raises right atrial pressure and opens the shunt, which is why the signals appear then.
exam2.hint: Consider which organ normally filters out injected bubbles.

exam2.question: Seventy-two hours after great saphenous vein ablation, duplex shows thrombus extending from the treated vein into the common femoral vein, filling about 30% of its lumen. Using the widely used SVS/AVF classification, which class of endothermal heat-induced thrombosis (EHIT) is this?

options.text: EHIT class 2
EHIT class 1
EHIT class 3
EHIT class 4

exam2.explanation: Class 1 thrombus reaches the junction without entering the deep vein; class 2 extends into the deep vein and fills 50% or less of its lumen; class 3 fills more than 50%; class 4 is occlusive DVT. Thrombus filling 30% of the common femoral vein is class 2.
exam2.hint: Check whether the thrombus enters the deep vein, and then how much of the lumen it fills.

exam2.question: Five days after liver transplantation, liver enzymes rise sharply. No hepatic arterial signal is detected in the porta hepatis or within the liver despite a low color scale, low wall filter and high gain, while portal vein flow is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis, and why is it serious?

options.text: Portal vein thrombosis, because it causes massive ascites
Mild hepatic artery stenosis, because it slowly reduces graft size
Hepatic artery thrombosis, because the bile ducts depend on arterial blood
Hepatic vein stenosis, because it causes congestion of the graft

exam2.explanation: Absent hepatic arterial flow with optimized settings after liver transplantation indicates hepatic artery thrombosis, the most serious vascular complication, because the transplanted bile ducts rely solely on hepatic arterial supply and can necrose. Portal vein flow is normal here, so portal vein thrombosis does not fit.
exam2.hint: Consider which blood supply the transplanted biliary tree depends on.

exam2.question: A 74-year-old woman has a transcranial Doppler exam. No signals can be found through either temporal window despite maximum power and gain, while the orbital and suboccipital windows give normal signals. How should this be reported?

options.text: Inadequate temporal windows, with the MCAs not assessed
Bilateral MCA occlusion
Severely raised intracranial pressure
Cerebral circulatory arrest

exam2.explanation: Temporal bone thickening often prevents insonation, especially in older women, so absent signals through that window mean the study is limited, not that the arteries are occluded. Normal signals through other windows argue strongly against circulatory arrest.
exam2.hint: Absence of signal is not the same as absence of flow.

exam2.question: A patient has had recurrent pulmonary emboli, but no DVT has been found. Duplex shows a fusiform dilation of the popliteal vein to 2.5 cm, more than twice its normal size, with swirling flow and no thrombus. What is the main clinical significance?

options.text: A popliteal venous aneurysm, an embolic source usually repaired surgically
A harmless anatomic variant that needs no further follow-up
A Baker cyst that should be drained under ultrasound guidance
A popliteal artery aneurysm that threatens limb ischemia

exam2.explanation: Popliteal venous aneurysms can form thrombus that embolizes even when the rest of the venous system is normal, so they are a recognized cause of otherwise unexplained PE and are usually repaired. The finding is in the vein with venous flow, so it is not an arterial aneurysm or a cyst.
exam2.hint: Link the swirling flow in the dilated vein to the patient's history of emboli.

exam2.question: Following the common hepatic artery from the celiac trunk toward the liver, the origin of which branch marks where it continues as the proper hepatic artery?

options.text: Left gastric artery
Splenic artery
Gastroduodenal artery
Inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery

exam2.explanation: The common hepatic artery runs to the right from the celiac trunk; after it gives off the gastroduodenal artery, which descends behind the first part of the duodenum near the pancreatic head, it continues as the proper hepatic artery into the porta hepatis. The left gastric and splenic arteries are celiac branches, and the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery arises from the SMA.
exam2.hint: Look for the branch that turns downward near the pancreatic head and is also a pancreatic landmark.

exam2.question: A painless lateral neck mass is found. Duplex shows a hypervascular solid mass high in the neck that pushes both the ICA and the ECA forward together, without separating them at the bifurcation. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.text: Carotid body tumor
Jugular vein thrombosis
Branchial cleft cyst
Vagal paraganglioma (glomus vagale)

exam2.explanation: A vagal paraganglioma arises from the vagus nerve, which lies behind the carotids, so it displaces both vessels anteriorly without splaying them. A carotid body tumor sits in the crotch of the bifurcation and spreads the ICA and ECA apart, and a branchial cleft cyst is avascular.
exam2.hint: Compare where the mass sits relative to the bifurcation and whether the vessels are pushed apart.

exam2.question: For a unilateral lower extremity venous duplex exam ordered for right leg symptoms, why is spectral Doppler of the left common femoral vein also recorded?

options.text: It serves as a complete screening exam for DVT in the left leg
Side-to-side comparison separates one-sided proximal obstruction from systemic causes
It is required to calculate the ankle-brachial index for that leg
It is used to measure the venous refill time in the opposite leg

exam2.explanation: Bilateral common femoral waveforms let the reader tell an asymmetric change, such as one-sided loss of phasicity from iliac obstruction, from a bilateral change such as pulsatility from heart failure. A single contralateral waveform does not exclude DVT in that leg.
exam2.hint: Consider what a single waveform cannot tell you unless there is something to compare it with.

exam2.question: In a patient with a duplicated inferior vena cava, how does the left-sided IVC usually drain?

options.text: Directly into the right atrium through a separate opening
Into the hemiazygos vein behind the left crus
Into the left gonadal vein in the pelvis
Into the left renal vein, which then crosses to the right IVC

exam2.explanation: A duplicated left IVC usually ascends on the left side of the aorta and ends in the left renal vein, which then crosses anterior to the aorta to join the right IVC. Recognizing it matters during IVC filter placement and when evaluating left-sided venous thrombosis.
exam2.hint: Follow the left renal vein, the usual path across the midline.

exam2.question: Both common carotid artery waveforms show two systolic peaks separated by a midsystolic dip in each cardiac cycle (a bisferiens pattern). Which cardiac condition is classically associated with this pattern?

options.text: Mitral valve stenosis
Isolated severe aortic stenosis
Complete heart block
Significant aortic regurgitation, often with aortic stenosis

exam2.explanation: A bisferiens pulse is seen with aortic regurgitation, especially combined aortic stenosis and regurgitation, and with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy. Isolated aortic stenosis produces a single delayed, rounded peak (tardus-parvus) instead.
exam2.hint: A large stroke volume ejected rapidly creates two peaks; an obstructed valve alone creates one slow one.

exam2.question: A patient with an IVC filter has new swelling of both legs, and both common femoral veins show continuous, nonphasic flow. Enlarged superficial veins are seen on the lower abdominal wall. If these are collaterals bypassing a caval occlusion, which flow pattern is expected in them?

options.text: Flow directed upward (cephalad) toward the chest wall veins, draining to the superior vena cava
Flow radiating outward from the umbilicus, fed by a recanalized paraumbilical vein
Flow directed downward toward the groin and into the femoral veins
Pulsatile arterial flow, indicating arteriovenous fistulas

exam2.explanation: With IVC obstruction, blood from the legs and pelvis reaches the heart through the superficial epigastric and thoracoepigastric veins to the axillary veins and superior vena cava, so lower abdominal wall veins flow upward. Below the umbilicus these veins normally drain downward to the groin. Flow radiating from the umbilicus through a paraumbilical vein indicates portal hypertension (caput medusae), not caval obstruction.
exam2.hint: Ask how blood from the legs can still reach the heart when the IVC is blocked.

exam2.question: A patient with a forearm loop PTFE dialysis graft has decreasing access flow and prolonged bleeding after needle removal. Where is a stenosis most likely to be found?

options.text: At the arterial anastomosis
At or just beyond the venous anastomosis
In the mid-graft cannulation zone
In the brachial artery above the elbow

exam2.explanation: The venous anastomosis and the outflow vein just beyond it are the most common sites of graft stenosis, caused by neointimal hyperplasia. An outflow stenosis raises pressure within the graft, which explains the prolonged bleeding after needle removal.
exam2.hint: Prolonged bleeding points to high pressure in the graft from narrowing downstream.

exam2.question: A patient received neck radiation for lymphoma 12 years ago. Which pattern of carotid disease is most typical of radiation-induced arteriopathy?

options.text: A beaded appearance of the distal cervical ICA
Long-segment disease of the CCA and other sites within the radiation field
Disease limited to the intracranial carotid siphon
A short focal plaque confined to the carotid bulb

exam2.explanation: Radiation damages the vessel wall throughout the treated field, causing diffuse, long-segment wall thickening and stenosis, often in the CCA and other unusual locations. Ordinary atherosclerosis tends to concentrate at the bulb and proximal ICA.
exam2.hint: The disease follows the radiation field rather than the usual sites of flow disturbance.

exam2.question: On postpartum day 4, a woman has fever and right-sided abdominal pain. Ultrasound shows a tubular, noncompressible structure with echogenic contents and no flow, running upward from the right adnexa toward the IVC. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Acute appendicitis
Right ovarian vein thrombosis
Right hydroureter
Right iliac artery aneurysm

exam2.explanation: Ovarian vein thrombosis occurs mainly after delivery, favors the right side, and appears as a thrombosed tubular vein extending from the adnexa toward the IVC. A dilated ureter is also tubular but contains anechoic urine and can be traced into the kidney, not toward the IVC.
exam2.hint: Note the timing after delivery and the direction in which the tube runs.

exam3.question: A carotid duplex exam shows visible plaque in the proximal left internal carotid artery with a peak systolic velocity of 265 cm/s, an end-diastolic velocity of 110 cm/s, and an ICA/CCA peak systolic velocity ratio of 4.6. Using SRU consensus criteria, how should this stenosis be graded?

options.text: Less than 50%
70% or greater, short of near occlusion
Total occlusion

exam3.explanation: An ICA PSV above 230 cm/s with visible plaque, supported by an ICA/CCA ratio above 4.0 and an EDV above 100 cm/s, falls in the 70% or greater category. The 50% to 69% category requires a PSV of 125 to 230 cm/s, which this velocity clearly exceeds.
exam3.hint: Compare the peak systolic velocity to the upper threshold of the SRU criteria.

exam3.question: A 68-year-old man has heterogeneous plaque in the right internal carotid artery bulb. The ICA peak systolic velocity is 158 cm/s, the end-diastolic velocity is 48 cm/s, and the ICA/CCA ratio is 2.6. Which SRU category best fits these findings?

options.text: Normal, no stenosis
Less than 50% stenosis
70% or greater stenosis
50% to 69% stenosis

exam3.explanation: A PSV between 125 and 230 cm/s with visible plaque, supported by an ICA/CCA ratio of 2 to 4 and an EDV of 40 to 100 cm/s, indicates a 50% to 69% stenosis. A PSV of 158 cm/s is well above the 125 cm/s threshold, so the less than 50% category does not apply.
exam3.hint: Locate 158 cm/s between the two SRU peak systolic velocity thresholds.

exam3.question: Which sonographic finding most reliably distinguishes the external carotid artery from the internal carotid artery?

options.text: Branch vessels arising from it in the neck
A larger diameter than the internal carotid artery
A low-resistance waveform with high diastolic flow
A posterolateral course relative to the internal carotid

exam3.explanation: The internal carotid artery normally has no branches in the neck, so demonstrating branches is the most definitive way to identify the ECA. The ECA has a high-resistance waveform, not a low-resistance one, and it typically lies anteromedial and is usually smaller than the ICA.
exam3.hint: Think about which of the two vessels gives off no extracranial branches.

exam3.question: During a carotid duplex exam, the left vertebral artery waveform shows a sharp mid-systolic deceleration that dips toward, but not below, the baseline, followed by antegrade flow in diastole. The right vertebral artery is normal. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: Complete subclavian steal from a left subclavian occlusion
Distal left vertebral artery occlusion near the basilar artery
Early (incomplete) subclavian steal from a proximal left subclavian stenosis
A normal variant of vertebral artery flow

exam3.explanation: A mid-systolic notch or deceleration with persistent antegrade flow is the earliest (latent or partial) stage of subclavian steal and indicates a hemodynamically significant proximal subclavian or innominate lesion. Complete steal produces fully reversed vertebral flow throughout the cardiac cycle, which is not described here.
exam3.hint: Consider how vertebral flow changes progressively as a proximal subclavian lesion worsens.

exam3.question: A vertebral artery shows a mid-systolic notch suggestive of a partial subclavian steal. Which maneuver is most useful to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Have the patient perform a Valsalva maneuver while monitoring the vertebral artery
Rotate the patient's head toward the side being examined
Inflate an arm cuff above systolic pressure for several minutes, then release it while monitoring the vertebral artery
Compress the ipsilateral common carotid artery for several seconds

exam3.explanation: Releasing an occluding arm cuff creates reactive hyperemia, lowering arm resistance and increasing demand, which accentuates or completes vertebral flow reversal if a steal is present. Carotid compression is not recommended and does not test the subclavian-to-vertebral pathway.
exam3.hint: The goal is to increase blood demand in the arm on the affected side.

exam3.question: Why do many laboratories use higher velocity thresholds to grade in-stent restenosis after carotid artery stenting than for a native internal carotid artery?

options.text: The stent reduces arterial wall compliance, which raises velocities even without significant narrowing
The stent struts cause aliasing that artificially lowers measured velocities
Stented arteries always develop compensatory dilation that lowers velocities
Doppler angle correction cannot be used inside a stent

exam3.explanation: A stented segment is stiffer than a native artery, so velocities tend to be higher for a given lumen size, and applying native criteria would overestimate restenosis. Stent struts do not lower velocities through aliasing, and angle correction is used in stents just as in native vessels.
exam3.hint: Consider how a metal scaffold changes the mechanical properties of the arterial wall.

exam3.question: During a transcranial Doppler exam through the transtemporal window, a signal at a depth of 45 mm is directed toward the transducer. Which artery is most likely being insonated?

options.text: Anterior cerebral artery
Basilar artery
Ophthalmic artery
Middle cerebral artery

exam3.explanation: The middle cerebral artery is found at roughly 30 to 60 mm through the transtemporal window with flow toward the transducer. The anterior cerebral artery lies deeper (about 60 to 75 mm) and flows away from the transducer, and the basilar artery is examined through the suboccipital window.
exam3.hint: Combine the window, the depth, and the flow direction.

exam3.question: A transcranial Doppler exam in a patient with a head injury shows markedly elevated pulsatility indices with very low diastolic velocities in all intracranial arteries on both sides. Which condition does this pattern most suggest?

options.text: Vasospasm of the middle cerebral arteries
Increased intracranial pressure
An intracranial arteriovenous malformation
Severe stenosis of one proximal internal carotid artery

exam3.explanation: Raised intracranial pressure increases resistance to cerebral perfusion globally, producing high pulsatility and low diastolic flow in every vessel. Vasospasm causes focal velocity elevation, while an AVM and a proximal ICA stenosis tend to lower pulsatility in the affected territory.
exam3.hint: A global, bilateral change points to a cause that affects the entire intracranial space.

exam3.question: A carotid plaque appears predominantly hypoechoic (echolucent) on gray-scale imaging. Which composition does this appearance most likely represent?

options.text: Dense calcification
Mature fibrous tissue
Organized collagen with calcium
Lipid-rich material or intraplaque hemorrhage

exam3.explanation: Echolucent plaque is associated with soft components such as lipid and intraplaque hemorrhage and is considered less stable with higher embolic potential. Calcification is highly echogenic and casts an acoustic shadow, and fibrous tissue is moderately to highly echogenic.
exam3.hint: Softer plaque components reflect less ultrasound.

exam3.question: A 42-year-old woman develops neck pain and a headache after chiropractic neck manipulation. Duplex shows no plaque, but the internal carotid artery lumen tapers smoothly beginning about 2 cm above the bulb, with a high-resistance waveform and little diastolic flow proximally. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Atherosclerotic occlusion at the carotid bifurcation
Internal carotid artery dissection
Carotid body tumor
Normal carotid sinus flow

exam3.explanation: A smooth, tapering lumen distal to the bulb without plaque in a younger patient with neck pain after trauma or manipulation is a classic presentation of spontaneous or traumatic ICA dissection. Atherosclerotic disease typically involves the bulb with visible plaque, which is absent here.
exam3.hint: Note the patient's age, the absence of plaque, and the precipitating event.

exam3.question: Which duplex finding is characteristic of fibromuscular dysplasia of the internal carotid artery?

options.text: Alternating areas of narrowing and dilation with velocity increases and turbulence in the mid-to-distal segment
Heavily calcified plaque with acoustic shadowing at the carotid bulb
A single smooth, long-segment narrowing of the common carotid artery
A hypoechoic mass splaying the internal and external carotid arteries

exam3.explanation: Fibromuscular dysplasia produces a string-of-beads pattern of webs and dilations, seen on duplex as segmental velocity elevation and turbulence, usually away from the bifurcation. Calcified bulb plaque is typical of atherosclerosis, and a mass splaying the bifurcation describes a carotid body tumor.
exam3.hint: Picture the classic angiographic appearance of this nonatherosclerotic disease.

exam3.question: A duplex exam 14 months after carotid endarterectomy shows a smooth, homogeneous narrowing at the endarterectomy site with elevated velocities. Which process is the most likely cause of restenosis at this time?

options.text: Recurrent atherosclerotic plaque
A retained intimal flap from surgery
Myointimal (neointimal) hyperplasia
Arterial wall calcification

exam3.explanation: Restenosis within about the first two years after endarterectomy is usually caused by myointimal hyperplasia, which appears smooth and homogeneous. Recurrent atherosclerosis is the typical cause of restenosis that develops later, usually after two years.
exam3.hint: Restenosis cause depends on how long it has been since surgery.

exam3.question: A patient has a known occlusion of the right internal carotid artery. The left internal carotid artery shows a peak systolic velocity of 145 cm/s with only minimal plaque, and the left CCA velocity is also elevated. Which explanation is most likely?

options.text: The left ICA must have a 70% or greater stenosis based on velocity alone
Left vertebral artery steal is lowering the left ICA velocity
Doppler angle error is the only possible explanation
Compensatory increased flow in the left carotid system may overestimate the degree of stenosis

exam3.explanation: When one ICA is occluded, the contralateral carotid often carries increased collateral flow, which raises velocities and can lead to overestimation of stenosis. Using the ICA/CCA ratio and the gray-scale plaque burden helps avoid overgrading in this situation.
exam3.hint: Consider where blood to the right hemisphere must come from.

exam3.question: A vertebral artery measures 1.8 mm in diameter and shows a high-resistance waveform with low diastolic flow, while the contralateral vertebral artery is large with normal low-resistance flow. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: A hypoplastic vertebral artery
Complete subclavian steal
Vertebral artery dissection with pseudoaneurysm
Severe stenosis of the contralateral vertebral artery origin

exam3.explanation: A small vertebral artery (generally under about 2 to 2.5 mm) with high-resistance flow and a large contralateral vessel is typical of vertebral hypoplasia. Subclavian steal produces reversed or notched flow rather than simply a small, high-resistance vessel.
exam3.hint: Compare the size and resistance of the two vertebral arteries.

exam3.question: Which artery is normally the first branch of the external carotid artery?

options.text: Facial artery
Superior thyroid artery
Superficial temporal artery
Ophthalmic artery

exam3.explanation: The superior thyroid artery usually arises from the anterior aspect of the proximal external carotid artery and is its first branch. The ophthalmic artery is the first major branch of the internal carotid artery, not the external carotid, and the superficial temporal is a terminal branch.
exam3.hint: Think about which branch arises most proximally from the anterior surface of the ECA, just above the bifurcation.

exam3.question: The tibioperoneal trunk normally divides into which two arteries?

options.text: Anterior tibial and peroneal arteries
Anterior tibial and posterior tibial arteries
Posterior tibial and peroneal arteries
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries

exam3.explanation: The popliteal artery gives off the anterior tibial artery first, then continues as the tibioperoneal trunk, which divides into the posterior tibial and peroneal arteries. The anterior tibial artery is not a branch of the trunk.
exam3.hint: Remember which tibial artery leaves the popliteal artery before the trunk forms.

exam3.question: At which anatomic landmark does the superficial femoral artery become the popliteal artery?

options.text: The inguinal ligament
The adductor hiatus
The origin of the profunda femoris artery
The knee joint line

exam3.explanation: The superficial femoral artery passes through the adductor (Hunter's) canal and becomes the popliteal artery as it exits through the adductor hiatus. The inguinal ligament marks the transition from the external iliac to the common femoral artery.
exam3.hint: Think about where the artery passes from the front of the thigh to the back of the knee.

exam3.question: The dorsalis pedis artery is the continuation of which artery?

options.text: Posterior tibial artery
Peroneal artery
Lateral plantar artery
Anterior tibial artery

exam3.explanation: The anterior tibial artery runs down the anterior compartment and continues onto the dorsum of the foot as the dorsalis pedis artery. The posterior tibial artery passes behind the medial malleolus and divides into the plantar arteries.
exam3.hint: Consider which leg artery ends on the top of the foot rather than passing behind the medial malleolus.

exam3.question: Which artery of the circle of Willis connects the internal carotid artery to the posterior cerebral artery?

options.text: Posterior communicating artery
Anterior communicating artery
Anterior cerebral artery
Superior cerebellar artery

exam3.explanation: The posterior communicating artery joins the internal carotid artery to the posterior cerebral artery, linking the anterior and posterior circulations. The anterior communicating artery connects the two anterior cerebral arteries.
exam3.hint: This vessel links the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems on each side.

exam3.question: In most people, the superficial palmar arch is supplied predominantly by which artery?

options.text: Radial artery
Interosseous artery
Ulnar artery
Brachial artery

exam3.explanation: The superficial palmar arch is formed mainly by the ulnar artery, with a smaller contribution from the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery. The deep palmar arch is the one formed mainly by the radial artery.
exam3.hint: The two forearm arteries each dominate a different palmar arch.

exam3.question: According to Poiseuille's law, if the radius of an artery is reduced by half while other factors remain constant, how does resistance to flow change?

options.text: It doubles
It increases 4 times
It increases 8 times
It increases 16 times

exam3.explanation: Resistance is inversely proportional to the radius raised to the fourth power, so halving the radius increases resistance by 2 to the fourth power, or 16 times. A fourfold increase would apply to area-based thinking, not the fourth-power relationship.
exam3.hint: Radius appears in Poiseuille's law raised to a power greater than two.

exam3.question: Based on the Bernoulli principle, what happens as blood enters a stenosis?

options.text: Velocity decreases and pressure increases
Velocity increases and pressure decreases
Velocity and pressure both increase
Velocity and pressure both remain constant

exam3.explanation: Within a narrowing, kinetic energy rises as velocity increases, so pressure energy must fall to keep total energy constant. This pressure drop across a stenosis is why velocity rises while distal pressure decreases.
exam3.hint: Total fluid energy is conserved, so a gain in one form must be offset by a loss in another.

exam3.question: At approximately what degree of narrowing does a stenosis typically become hemodynamically significant, reducing pressure and flow at resting flow rates?

options.text: 50% diameter reduction, about 75% area reduction
20% diameter reduction, about 35% area reduction
30% diameter reduction, about 50% area reduction
90% diameter reduction, about 99% area reduction

exam3.explanation: A critical stenosis is generally reached at about a 50% diameter or 75% cross-sectional area reduction, when a measurable pressure and flow drop begins at rest. A 90% narrowing is well beyond the threshold, not the point at which significance begins.
exam3.hint: Area reduction is always greater than diameter reduction for the same lesion.

exam3.question: A spectral Doppler waveform is obtained in an artery a few centimeters proximal to a complete occlusion with no intervening branches. Which waveform pattern is most expected?

options.text: Low-resistance flow with increased diastolic velocities
Tardus-parvus flow with a delayed systolic upstroke
Markedly elevated velocities with post-stenotic turbulence
High-resistance flow with diminished or absent diastolic flow and reduced velocities

exam3.explanation: Proximal to an occlusion, outflow resistance is very high, so the waveform becomes high resistance with little or no diastolic flow and often low velocities. A tardus-parvus pattern is seen distal, not proximal, to a significant obstruction.
exam3.hint: Think about the resistance the blood encounters just ahead of a blocked segment.

exam3.question: Where is post-stenotic turbulence, with spectral broadening and simultaneous forward and reverse flow, best demonstrated?

options.text: Several centimeters proximal to the stenosis
At the narrowest point of the stenotic jet only
Immediately distal to the stenosis, within about 1 to 2 cm
Far downstream in the distal outflow arteries

exam3.explanation: Flow exiting a stenotic jet becomes disturbed just beyond the narrowing, producing spectral broadening and bidirectional flow within roughly the first 1 to 2 cm. The narrowest point shows the highest velocity jet, not the disturbed flow, and flow becomes laminar again farther downstream.
exam3.hint: Disturbed flow forms as the high-velocity jet expands into the wider lumen.

exam3.question: Two moderate stenoses are present in series along the same arterial segment. Neither would be hemodynamically significant alone. Which statement best describes their combined effect?

options.text: Their resistances add, so together they may produce a significant pressure drop
Only the more severe lesion affects pressure, so the other can be ignored
Their combined resistance is lower than either lesion alone
Lesions in series cancel each other's effect on distal flow

exam3.explanation: Resistances in series are additive, so tandem lesions can together reduce distal pressure and flow significantly even when each is moderate. Combined resistance lower than either component applies to vessels arranged in parallel, not in series.
exam3.hint: Recall how resistances combine when arranged one after another.

exam3.question: In a healthy individual, how does ankle systolic pressure respond immediately after treadmill exercise?

options.text: It drops sharply and takes more than 10 minutes to recover
It stays the same or rises slightly
It falls to near zero for several minutes
It becomes unobtainable due to vasospasm

exam3.explanation: In a normal limb, exercise-induced vasodilation is matched by increased inflow, so ankle pressure is maintained or slightly increased. A significant post-exercise drop with delayed recovery indicates arterial occlusive disease.
exam3.hint: A normal arterial system can meet increased demand without losing pressure.

exam3.question: Why are ankle and arm pressures for the ankle-brachial index measured with the patient supine?

options.text: To increase peripheral resistance in the legs
To make the posterior tibial artery easier to compress
To reduce the effect of respiration on arterial pressure
To eliminate hydrostatic pressure differences between the arm and the ankle

exam3.explanation: When standing, the ankle sits well below the heart and gains substantial hydrostatic pressure, which would falsely raise ankle pressure. Placing the patient supine puts the arm and ankle at nearly the same level relative to the heart.
exam3.hint: Consider the weight of the blood column between the heart and the foot.

exam3.question: What is the correct technique for measuring the maximum diameter of an abdominal aortic aneurysm on ultrasound?

options.text: Inner wall to inner wall of the residual flow lumen only
Along an oblique plane that includes the longest length of the sac
Outer wall to outer wall, perpendicular to the long axis of the aorta
From the anterior wall to the spine in a sagittal view

exam3.explanation: AAA diameter is measured from the outer wall to the outer wall, perpendicular to the vessel's true axis, so thrombus is included and obliquity does not exaggerate the size. Measuring only the flow lumen would underestimate aneurysm size because mural thrombus is excluded.
exam3.hint: Think about what the measurement must include to reflect the aneurysm's true size and rupture risk.

exam3.question: What is the most common complication of a popliteal artery aneurysm?

options.text: Thrombosis or distal embolization causing limb ischemia
Rupture into the popliteal fossa
Compression of the tibial nerve causing foot drop
Arteriovenous fistula with the popliteal vein

exam3.explanation: Popliteal aneurysms most often present with thrombosis or embolization to the tibial arteries, which can threaten the limb. Unlike abdominal aortic aneurysms, rupture is uncommon.
exam3.hint: Unlike the aorta, this aneurysm rarely bursts.

exam3.question: A patient develops a pulsatile groin mass after femoral artery catheterization. Duplex shows a rounded sac with swirling color flow connected to the artery by a narrow tract. What spectral Doppler pattern is expected within that tract?

options.text: Continuous low-resistance flow from the artery into an adjacent vein
Absent flow because the tract is thrombosed
Monophasic high-velocity flow only in diastole
To-and-fro flow, toward the sac in systole and back to the artery in diastole

exam3.explanation: The neck of a pseudoaneurysm shows a characteristic to-and-fro pattern as blood enters the sac in systole and exits in diastole. Continuous low-resistance flow into a vein is the hallmark of an arteriovenous fistula instead.
exam3.hint: Blood that fills the sac during systole has to leave it during diastole.

exam3.question: A 24-year-old runner reports calf claudication. Resting pedal pulses and popliteal waveforms are normal, but the popliteal waveform becomes markedly dampened during active plantar flexion of the foot. Which condition is most likely?

options.text: Thromboangiitis obliterans
Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome
Atherosclerotic superficial femoral artery occlusion
Chronic deep venous insufficiency

exam3.explanation: In popliteal entrapment, the artery is compressed by an abnormal relationship with the medial head of the gastrocnemius, so flow decreases with active plantar flexion or passive dorsiflexion. A young athlete with normal resting studies makes atherosclerosis unlikely.
exam3.hint: The findings change with a specific calf muscle contraction.

exam3.question: A patient with cold-induced finger color changes has digit photoplethysmography performed at room temperature. Several fingers show flattened, low-amplitude waveforms that remain abnormal after the hands are warmed. What do these findings suggest?

options.text: Primary vasospastic Raynaud's with no fixed obstruction
Normal digital perfusion
Fixed obstructive digital artery disease
Venous outflow obstruction of the hand

exam3.explanation: Waveforms that stay flattened after warming indicate a fixed obstruction, as seen with secondary (obstructive) Raynaud's from conditions such as connective tissue disease. In primary vasospastic Raynaud's, waveforms normalize once the hands are warmed.
exam3.hint: Consider whether warming removed the abnormality.

exam3.question: When do most stenoses that threaten the patency of an infrainguinal vein bypass graft develop, and what is the usual cause?

options.text: Within the first 1 to 2 years, from intimal hyperplasia
Within the first 24 hours, from recurrent atherosclerosis
After 10 years, from intimal hyperplasia
Within the first 1 to 2 years, from graft aneurysm formation

exam3.explanation: Most graft-threatening lesions form in the first one to two years at anastomoses and valve sites due to intimal hyperplasia, which is why surveillance is most frequent early. Failure in the first days usually reflects technical problems, and late failures are mostly due to progression of atherosclerosis.
exam3.hint: Surveillance is most frequent during the period when this lesion is most likely.

exam3.question: A diabetic patient has a right ankle pressure of 220 mmHg, a brachial pressure of 130 mmHg, and a right great toe pressure of 28 mmHg. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Normal arterial perfusion because the ABI is greater than 1.0
Significant arterial disease, with the ABI falsely elevated by noncompressible tibial arteries
Mild disease limited to the aortoiliac segment
Venous hypertension causing an artificially high ankle pressure

exam3.explanation: An ABI above 1.3 to 1.4 in a diabetic patient suggests medial calcification, making the ABI unreliable, while a toe pressure of 28 mmHg indicates markedly reduced perfusion. Digital arteries are less often calcified, so the toe pressure is the more accurate measure here.
exam3.hint: Decide which of the measurements is not affected by vessel calcification.

exam3.question: For an asymptomatic man with an abdominal aortic aneurysm, at what maximum diameter is elective repair generally recommended?

options.text: 3.0 cm
4.0 cm
7.0 cm
5.5 cm

exam3.explanation: Guidelines generally recommend elective repair for asymptomatic AAA in men at 5.5 cm, when rupture risk outweighs operative risk; rapid growth or symptoms are also indications. A diameter of 3.0 cm defines an aneurysm but is managed with surveillance.
exam3.hint: This threshold is well above the size that defines an aneurysm.

exam3.question: A 45-year-old man with no atherosclerotic risk factors has calf claudication. Duplex shows a hypoechoic, fluid-filled structure within the wall of the popliteal artery that compresses the lumen. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Adventitial cystic disease of the popliteal artery
Popliteal artery aneurysm with mural thrombus
Baker's cyst compressing the popliteal vein
Popliteal artery dissection from trauma

exam3.explanation: Adventitial cystic disease is a rare condition in which a mucin-filled cyst forms within the arterial wall, narrowing the lumen and causing claudication in middle-aged men. A Baker's cyst lies outside the vessels, posteromedially between muscle tendons, and does not arise in the arterial wall.
exam3.hint: The cystic structure is located inside the arterial wall itself.

exam3.question: If the Doppler insonation angle changes from 0 degrees to 60 degrees while all other factors remain constant, how does the Doppler frequency shift change?

options.text: It doubles
It stays the same
It decreases by half
It falls to zero

exam3.explanation: The Doppler shift is proportional to the cosine of the angle; cos 0 is 1 and cos 60 is 0.5, so the shift is halved. The shift would fall to zero only at 90 degrees, where cosine equals zero.
exam3.hint: Compare the cosine values of the two angles.

exam3.question: Why is a Doppler angle of 60 degrees or less recommended when measuring velocities?

options.text: Angles below 60 degrees eliminate aliasing completely
At steeper angles, small angle-correction errors cause large velocity errors
Steeper angles always produce a higher Doppler shift
The wall filter only works at angles under 60 degrees

exam3.explanation: The cosine changes rapidly as the angle approaches 90 degrees, so a slight misalignment of the angle cursor produces a large error in calculated velocity. Steeper angles actually produce smaller, not larger, Doppler shifts.
exam3.hint: Think about how quickly the cosine curve changes near 90 degrees.

exam3.question: Aliasing is seen on a pulsed-wave Doppler spectrum from a stenotic artery. Which adjustment would NOT help eliminate the aliasing?

options.text: Increasing the velocity scale (PRF)
Lowering the spectral baseline
Using a lower-frequency transducer
Switching to a higher-frequency transducer

exam3.explanation: A higher transmitted frequency produces a larger Doppler shift, making aliasing worse. Raising the scale, shifting the baseline, and lowering transducer frequency all help display higher velocities without wraparound.
exam3.hint: Consider how transmitted frequency affects the size of the Doppler shift.

exam3.question: What is the main risk of setting the wall filter too high during a peripheral arterial Doppler exam?

options.text: Peak systolic velocities will be falsely increased
Aliasing will appear at lower velocities
Low-velocity diastolic flow may be removed, making the waveform appear more resistive or absent
Spectral broadening will be exaggerated

exam3.explanation: The wall filter rejects low-frequency shifts, so an excessive setting can erase slow diastolic flow and mimic high resistance or even occlusion with very low flow. It does not change the Nyquist limit or raise peak velocity.
exam3.hint: The filter removes signals below a chosen frequency.

exam3.question: Which pulsed-wave Doppler setting is most likely to cause artifactual spectral broadening in a normal artery?

options.text: A large sample volume spanning the entire lumen
A small sample volume centered in the lumen
Decreasing the Doppler gain
Increasing the wall filter

exam3.explanation: A sample volume that includes slower flow near the walls along with fast central flow records a wide range of velocities, filling the spectral window. A small, centered sample volume samples mainly the fast central flow and produces a clear window in a normal vessel.
exam3.hint: Consider which setting samples the widest range of velocities across the vessel.

exam3.question: An internal carotid artery appears occluded on color Doppler. Which adjustment best helps detect a trickle of very slow flow before calling it occluded?

options.text: Increasing the color velocity scale
Increasing the color wall filter
Decreasing the color gain
Decreasing the color velocity scale

exam3.explanation: Lowering the color scale (PRF) increases sensitivity to slow flow, which is essential for separating a near occlusion from a true occlusion. Raising the scale or wall filter and reducing gain all reduce sensitivity to low-velocity flow.
exam3.hint: Optimize the system for the slowest possible flow.

exam3.question: During ultrasound-guided thrombin injection of a femoral pseudoaneurysm, where should the needle tip be positioned?

options.text: Within the pseudoaneurysm sac, away from the neck
Directly in the neck of the pseudoaneurysm
In the native femoral artery just below the neck
In the subcutaneous tissue superficial to the sac

exam3.explanation: Placing the needle tip in the sac away from the neck reduces the risk of thrombin escaping into the native artery and causing distal thrombosis. Injecting in the neck or native artery is the most dangerous position for this reason.
exam3.hint: The goal is to keep the thrombin out of the native circulation.

exam3.question: During great saphenous vein mapping before a lower extremity bypass, which technique best distends the vein to obtain accurate diameter measurements?

options.text: Placing the patient in Trendelenburg position
Placing the patient in reverse Trendelenburg or a dependent position
Having the patient perform repeated calf contractions
Applying firm transducer pressure over the vein

exam3.explanation: A dependent or reverse Trendelenburg position increases venous filling, so the vein is measured at its distended diameter, which better reflects its usefulness as a conduit. Trendelenburg empties the leg veins, and transducer pressure compresses the vein and underestimates diameter.
exam3.hint: Use gravity to fill the vein.

exam3.question: During a duplex follow-up exam after superficial femoral artery stenting, which protocol is most appropriate?

options.text: Record a single velocity from the mid stent only
Image only the outflow artery because stents rarely narrow internally
Evaluate the inflow artery, the proximal, mid, and distal stent, and the outflow artery
Measure only the ankle-brachial index without imaging the stent

exam3.explanation: In-stent restenosis and edge stenoses can occur anywhere along the stent or at its ends, so velocities are recorded in the inflow, throughout the stent, and in the outflow to calculate velocity ratios. A single mid-stent sample can miss focal narrowing at the stent edges.
exam3.hint: Restenosis often develops at the ends of the stent as well as within it.

exam3.question: A 72-year-old man had a 20-minute episode of left arm weakness and slurred speech that fully resolved. Which noninvasive vascular test should be ordered first?

options.text: Lower extremity arterial duplex
Upper extremity venous duplex
Segmental pressures of the arms
Carotid duplex ultrasound

exam3.explanation: Transient focal hemispheric symptoms such as unilateral weakness and speech difficulty suggest a carotid source, so carotid duplex is the appropriate first test. Arm segmental pressures assess arm arterial disease, not a cerebral embolic source.
exam3.hint: These symptoms point to one cerebral hemisphere and its arterial supply.

exam3.question: A 65-year-old smoker reports reproducible calf pain with walking that resolves with rest. Which test is most appropriate as the initial noninvasive evaluation?

options.text: Contrast angiography of the lower extremities
Ankle-brachial index with segmental pressures
Lower extremity venous reflux study
Transcranial Doppler

exam3.explanation: Physiologic testing with the ABI and segmental pressures is the standard first step to confirm PAD and estimate its level and severity. Angiography is invasive and reserved for planning intervention.
exam3.hint: Start with the simplest physiologic test that confirms and localizes disease.

exam3.question: Which clinical finding is an appropriate indication for a carotid duplex exam?

options.text: Calf claudication after walking two blocks
Unilateral leg swelling after a long flight
A cervical bruit heard over the carotid bifurcation
Bilateral ankle edema with varicose veins

exam3.explanation: A neck bruit can signal carotid bifurcation stenosis and is an accepted indication for carotid duplex. Calf claudication suggests lower extremity arterial disease, and leg swelling or varicosities call for venous studies.
exam3.hint: Choose the finding that points to the neck arteries.

exam3.question: During a lower extremity venous duplex exam, two separate femoral vein channels are seen alongside the femoral artery in the mid-thigh. What is the most important implication of this finding?

options.text: It indicates chronic post-thrombotic recanalization
It is a common variant, and each channel must be compressed separately
It means the great saphenous vein has been mistaken for a deep vein
It is a rare anomaly that requires venography to confirm

exam3.explanation: Duplication of the femoral vein is a common normal variant, and thrombus can be confined to one of the two channels, so each one must be compressed and assessed separately. Recanalization after DVT produces several small irregular channels within a thick-walled vein, not two smooth, normal-sized veins.
exam3.hint: Think about how a clot could be missed if only one channel is examined.

exam3.question: In a transverse view of the medial thigh, the great saphenous vein lies within the saphenous compartment (the 'saphenous eye'). Which structures form the boundaries of this compartment?

options.text: The skin superficially and the femoral artery deep
The sartorius muscle superficially and the adductor longus deep
The subcutaneous fat superficially and the femoral vein deep
The saphenous fascia superficially and the muscular fascia deep

exam3.explanation: The great saphenous vein runs in a fascial compartment bounded by the saphenous (superficial) fascia above and the deep muscular fascia below, which gives the classic eye-shaped appearance in transverse. Tributaries and accessory veins lie outside this compartment in the subcutaneous fat, which helps tell them apart from the true GSV.
exam3.hint: Think about the echogenic layers that outline the 'eye' around the vein in a transverse view.

exam3.question: The perforating veins of the medial lower leg (historically called Cockett perforators) usually connect which two veins?

options.text: The posterior accessory great saphenous (posterior arch) vein and the posterior tibial veins
The small saphenous vein and the peroneal veins
The anterior accessory saphenous vein and the femoral vein
The great saphenous vein and the anterior tibial veins

exam3.explanation: The medial calf perforators, now called posterior tibial perforators, join the posterior arch vein (posterior accessory GSV) to the posterior tibial veins. Their incompetence is closely linked to medial ankle skin changes and venous ulcers; the anterior tibial veins lie in the anterior compartment and are not their usual connection.
exam3.hint: Their modern name tells you which deep veins they drain into.

exam3.question: A cranial extension of the small saphenous vein that runs up the posterior thigh and joins the great saphenous vein is known as which vessel?

options.text: Vein of Leonardo
Anterior accessory saphenous vein
Giacomini vein
Gastrocnemius vein

exam3.explanation: The Giacomini vein (intersaphenous vein) is a thigh extension of the small saphenous vein that connects to the great saphenous vein, and it can carry reflux between the two systems. The vein of Leonardo is the posterior arch vein in the calf, not a thigh connection.
exam3.hint: This vein links the two saphenous systems in the posterior thigh.

exam3.question: At which anatomic landmark does the axillary vein become the subclavian vein?

options.text: The lateral border of the first rib
The lower border of the teres major muscle
The sternoclavicular joint
The medial border of the scapula

exam3.explanation: The axillary vein becomes the subclavian vein as it crosses the lateral border of the first rib. The lower border of the teres major is where the brachial and basilic veins join to form the axillary vein, and the subclavian and internal jugular veins join behind the sternoclavicular joint.
exam3.hint: The same bony landmark divides the matching arterial segments.

exam3.question: The paired gastrocnemius veins normally drain into which vein?

options.text: Peroneal vein
Popliteal vein
Great saphenous vein
Anterior tibial vein

exam3.explanation: The gastrocnemius veins come out of the medial and lateral heads of the gastrocnemius muscle and drain into the popliteal vein, often near the small saphenous junction. The soleal sinuses, by contrast, drain mainly into the posterior tibial and peroneal veins.
exam3.hint: The gastrocnemius muscle starts above the knee, behind it.

exam3.question: In a transverse view of the proximal thigh, a superficial vein lies anterior to the femoral artery and vein and lines up directly over them. Which vein does this 'alignment sign' identify?

options.text: Great saphenous vein
Posterior accessory saphenous vein
Deep femoral vein
Anterior accessory saphenous vein

exam3.explanation: The anterior accessory saphenous vein runs lateral to the GSV and lies directly over the femoral artery and vein, which is called the alignment sign. The great saphenous vein lies more medially, in its own saphenous compartment, and does not line up with the femoral vessels.
exam3.hint: The great saphenous vein itself sits more medially, within its own fascial compartment.

exam3.question: A patient referred for leg swelling has bilaterally patent, compressible deep veins, but the common femoral vein Doppler signals are markedly pulsatile on both sides and change with each heartbeat. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Bilateral iliac vein obstruction
Bilateral great saphenous vein reflux
Elevated central venous pressure, such as from right heart failure
Normal flow in a patient holding their breath

exam3.explanation: Elevated right atrial pressure, as in right heart failure, tricuspid regurgitation or fluid overload, sends cardiac pulsations back into the peripheral veins and makes the waveforms pulsatile on both sides. Bilateral iliac obstruction would instead cause continuous flow with little phasicity.
exam3.hint: Consider what cardiac-synchronous changes seen in both legs say about where the problem lies.

exam3.question: In a healthy person, standing ankle venous pressure is about 90 mmHg. What normally happens to this pressure during walking?

options.text: It falls to about 20 to 30 mmHg because the calf muscle pump empties the veins
It rises to about 150 mmHg because muscle contraction squeezes the veins
It does not change because hydrostatic pressure depends only on height
It falls to zero and stays there until the person sits down

exam3.explanation: With competent valves, repeated calf muscle contraction empties the deep veins, and the valves stop the column from refilling right away, so ambulatory venous pressure falls to about 20 to 30 mmHg. In venous insufficiency this drop is much smaller (ambulatory venous hypertension), which drives skin changes and ulcers.
exam3.hint: Consider what the calf muscle pump and competent valves achieve together.

exam3.question: During a standing reflux study, rapid calf compression and release produces 0.8 seconds of retrograde flow in the popliteal vein. How should this be interpreted?

options.text: Pathologic deep venous reflux
Within normal limits for the popliteal vein
Evidence of popliteal vein obstruction
Indeterminate unless the duration exceeds 3 seconds

exam3.explanation: The widely used cut-off for femoral and popliteal vein reflux is more than 1 second, so 0.8 seconds is within normal limits. The 0.5 second cut-off applies to the superficial veins, deep calf veins and deep femoral vein, which is why calling this reflux would be a mistake.
exam3.hint: Recall that reflux duration cut-offs differ depending on which vein segment is tested.

exam3.question: Which technique is most appropriate for testing popliteal vein valve competence?

options.text: Patient supine, with gentle sustained thigh compression
Patient supine, during quiet breathing only
Patient prone with the knee fully extended, during deep inspiration
Patient standing or in steep reverse Trendelenburg, with rapid distal compression and release

exam3.explanation: Reflux testing needs gravity to load the valves, so the patient stands (or lies in steep reverse Trendelenburg) with the leg relaxed, and a rapid distal squeeze or cuff deflation is released to provoke retrograde flow. Testing supine during quiet breathing leaves the valves unloaded and causes false-negative results.
exam3.hint: Valves are tested best when gravity is pulling blood backward.

exam3.question: Deep vein thrombi most often begin in which location within the vein, and why?

options.text: At the saphenofemoral junction, where flow velocity is highest
Within the media of the vein wall, where smooth muscle is thickest
In the valve sinuses behind the cusps, where slow, swirling flow causes local stasis
In the center of the lumen, where shear stress is greatest

exam3.explanation: Behind each valve cusp, blood forms slow vortices, and this local stasis (one element of Virchow's triad) makes the valve sinus the usual starting point for DVT, especially in the calf veins. Fast, high-shear flow discourages thrombus formation rather than promoting it.
exam3.hint: Recall which element of Virchow's triad relates to blood flow.

exam3.question: Veins hold most of the circulating blood volume and are called capacitance vessels. Which property best explains this?

options.text: Thick muscular walls that resist stretching
High compliance, so they can take in large volume changes with little change in pressure
High resistance to flow compared with arterioles
A rigid circular cross-section at all pressures

exam3.explanation: Veins have thin walls and are highly compliant: at low pressure they are elliptical, and they become round as they fill, taking in large volumes with little rise in pressure. Thick muscular walls and high resistance describe arteries and arterioles, not veins.
exam3.hint: Think about how a partly collapsed vein changes shape as it fills.

exam3.question: Which spectral Doppler pattern is expected in a normal hepatic vein?

options.text: Multiphasic flow that is mostly away from the liver, with a brief reversal during atrial contraction
Continuous, low-velocity flow toward the liver with no pulsatility
High-resistance flow with absent diastolic flow
Low-resistance arterial flow with continuous diastolic flow

exam3.explanation: Normal hepatic veins mirror right atrial pressure changes: there are two antegrade waves (S and D) toward the heart and a brief retrograde a wave during atrial contraction, which gives a triphasic or multiphasic pattern. Continuous, low-velocity hepatopetal flow describes the normal portal vein.
exam3.hint: The hepatic veins sit right next to the right atrium.

exam3.question: A patient with 3 days of calf pain has a popliteal vein that does not compress. It is distended, larger than the adjacent artery, and filled with hypoechoic material that has a smooth border and seems only loosely attached to the wall. What do these findings suggest?

options.text: Chronic post-thrombotic change
Popliteal artery aneurysm with mural thrombus
Slow flow artifact (rouleaux formation)
Acute deep vein thrombosis

exam3.explanation: Acute thrombus is usually hypoechoic, distends the vein, and is soft or loosely attached, sometimes with a free-floating tail. Chronic thrombus is echogenic, the vein is often small or contracted, and the walls are thickened, irregular and firmly attached.
exam3.hint: Consider the vein's size and how echogenic the material is.

exam3.question: A patient with a DVT 2 years ago returns for a follow-up duplex scan. Which finding best fits chronic post-thrombotic change rather than new acute thrombus?

options.text: A distended vein filled with anechoic material
A free-floating, mobile thrombus tail
Thickened, echogenic vein walls with intraluminal bands (synechiae) and partial compression
A vein diameter twice that of the adjacent artery

exam3.explanation: Chronic post-thrombotic change shows thick, echogenic walls, webs or synechiae, a contracted or partly recanalized lumen, and often collaterals. A distended vein, anechoic or hypoechoic material and a free-floating tail are features of acute thrombus.
exam3.hint: Old thrombus becomes organized and scarred.

exam3.question: While scanning the common femoral vein, the sonographer sees a long, mobile thrombus tail moving freely within the lumen. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Avoid further compression of that segment and notify the interpreting physician promptly
Apply firm compression repeatedly to confirm the thrombus is attached
Have the patient perform a Valsalva maneuver to measure reflux
Finish the full bilateral reflux protocol before reporting

exam3.explanation: A free-floating thrombus is at risk of breaking off and embolizing, so extra compression should be kept to a minimum and the finding reported right away as urgent. Repeated forceful compression or provocative maneuvers could dislodge the thrombus.
exam3.hint: Think about what could cause the clot to embolize.

exam3.question: Superficial thrombophlebitis is found in the great saphenous vein, with the thrombus tip 2 cm from the saphenofemoral junction. Why is it important to document this distance?

options.text: Thrombus near the junction always resolves without treatment
Thrombus close to the junction carries a higher risk of extending into the deep system and is often treated like a DVT
The distance is needed only to plan cosmetic sclerotherapy
Thrombus within 5 cm of the junction rules out deep vein involvement
